written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: On that spring evening in Istanbul, when the Bosphorus was painted in shades of amber and violet, I handed my father the manuscript of "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" with trembling hands that betrayed both hope and terror. The pages, worn from countless revisions and bearing the weight of my artistic ambitions, disappeared into his leather briefcase – the same briefcase I had watched him carry to his office countless times throughout my childhood. In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man, examining the faces of passersby as if they might offer some preview of my father's judgment. Unlike my mother, who had always viewed my literary aspirations with the kind of worried skepticism reserved for a child's dangerous games, my father had maintained a curious silence about my choice to abandon architecture for the solitary life of a novelist. I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains, wondering if I had disappointed him. When he finally returned home that evening, before any words could form between us, he embraced me with an intensity that spoke volumes in our family's language of unspoken emotions. Later, as we sat in his study surrounded by his beloved books – the ones that had first taught me to love literature – he broke our emotional silence with words that would echo through the decades: "You will win great prizes one day." That moment hung between us like a photograph yellowing with age, gaining new meaning after his death in 2002, when I found myself standing alone in that same study, running my fingers along the spines of his books, feeling the weight of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.
written_by_MFA003.Reason: Both the original excerpt and excerpt 2 describe the return of the father and place some importance and relevance to it. in the first excerpt the wrier says that his father was far away and he had to wait for his return to hand him his novel for approval. In excerpt 2, the writer begins by stating that his father had just returned when he handed over the novel. There is however no mention of any return of the writer's father in excerpt 1
written_by_MFA003.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: The weight of the manuscript, a physical embodiment of years of creative struggle, felt familiar and foreign in my hands.  I had poured my heart and soul into "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," a tale woven from the rich tapestry of Istanbul's history and the intricate lives of its inhabitants.  The city, my muse and my prison, had borne witness to my solitary journey as a writer, a path I had chosen despite the uncertainties that gnawed at my soul.My father, unlike my mother, had always encouraged my artistic pursuits, seeing in them a reflection of his own unfulfilled dreams.  He had been a source of quiet strength, a steady hand on my shoulder as I navigated the treacherous waters of self-expression.  His return from Paris, a city that had both beckoned and betrayed him, had been a turning point in our relationship.The silence that followed my presentation of the manuscript was thick with unspoken emotions.  My father's embrace, a gesture of paternal affection and unspoken approval, had eased the anxieties that had plagued me for years.  His words, when they finally came, were filled with a conviction that surprised and humbled me."You will win the Nobel Prize one day," he had declared, his voice echoing with a certainty that transcended the boundaries of fatherly pride.The memory of that moment, etched into the deepest recesses of my mind, had become a source of solace and inspiration in the years that followed.  My father's belief in my abilities, his unwavering support for my artistic ambitions, had sustained me through the inevitable doubts and setbacks that litter the path of any creative endeavor.Even now, years after his passing in 2002, the echo of his words continues to resonate within me, a reminder of the enduring power of familial love and the transformative potential of artistic expression.

The city, my muse and my prison, had borne witness to my solitary journey as a writer, a path I had chosen despite the uncertainties that gnawed at my soul.My father, unlike my mother, had always encouraged my artistic pursuits, seeing in them a reflection of his own unfulfilled dreams.  He had been a source of quiet strength, a steady hand on my shoulder as I navigated the treacherous waters of self-expression.  His return from Paris, a city that had both beckoned and betrayed him, had been a turning point in our relationship.The silence that followed my presentation of the manuscript was thick with unspoken emotions.  My father's embrace, a gesture of paternal affection and unspoken approval, had eased the anxieties that had plagued me for years.  His words, when they finally came, were filled with a conviction that surprised and humbled me."You will win the Nobel Prize one day," he had declared, his voice echoing with a certainty that transcended the boundaries of fatherly pride.The memory of that moment, etched into the deepest recesses of my mind, had become a source of solace and inspiration in the years that followed.  My father's belief in my abilities, his unwavering support for my artistic ambitions, had sustained me through the inevitable doubts and setbacks that litter the path of any creative endeavor.Even now, years after his passing in 2002, the echo of his words continues to resonate within me, a reminder of the enduring power of familial love and the transformative potential of artistic expression.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: Sitting down to reflect on my life makes everything fall silent around me. I remember that I had committed to becoming a novelist at a very young age. My domestic circumstances were somewhat fortunate: although my mother believed I could commit myself to more useful professions like law and medicine, my father had always supported my ambition to become a writer. But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Excerpt 1 matches the style of the original more in that the father seems more open and enthusiastic with his praise and admiration, saying out loud how the narrator will win 'the Nobel Prize one day.' The conviction of this character is not portrayed in Excerpt 2 as the father 'refused to talk about the manuscript' for a few days and 'didn't name a prize'. This changes the dynamic between the two main characters too much compared to the original and does not match the voice or style.
written_by_MFA010.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

But one memory of my father is more significant than the rest. I remember that when, as a young man, I wrote my first novel, “Cevdet Bay and His Sons,” I sent a copy to my father for his opinion. Till I heard back from him, my days were consumed by the anxiety of what he might have to say. I came to care for my father’s opinion and approval more than anyone else’s. I had been waiting for my father to return home. I wanted to know his thoughts. On the day of his arrival, I stood by the door of our house and looked at him like I was nothing more than a child. My father must have understood what I was asking him. He walked up to me and embraced me. Although he didn’t say a word, I understood that he approved of my manuscript. For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_MFA010.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

The city, my muse and my prison, had borne witness to my solitary journey as a writer, a path I had chosen despite the uncertainties that gnawed at my soul.My father, unlike my mother, had always encouraged my artistic pursuits, seeing in them a reflection of his own unfulfilled dreams.  He had been a source of quiet strength, a steady hand on my shoulder as I navigated the treacherous waters of self-expression.  His return from Paris, a city that had both beckoned and betrayed him, had been a turning point in our relationship.The silence that followed my presentation of the manuscript was thick with unspoken emotions.  My father's embrace, a gesture of paternal affection and unspoken approval, had eased the anxieties that had plagued me for years.  His words, when they finally came, were filled with a conviction that surprised and humbled me."You will win the Nobel Prize one day," he had declared, his voice echoing with a certainty that transcended the boundaries of fatherly pride.The memory of that moment, etched into the deepest recesses of my mind, had become a source of solace and inspiration in the years that followed.  My father's belief in my abilities, his unwavering support for my artistic ambitions, had sustained me through the inevitable doubts and setbacks that litter the path of any creative endeavor.Even now, years after his passing in 2002, the echo of his words continues to resonate within me, a reminder of the enduring power of familial love and the transformative potential of artistic expression.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. After Aunt Nell died (a quick death, heart attack while hanging laundry), the summer visits stopped, though Christmas cards arrived without fail, bearing generic winter scenes and his meticulously penned signature. Years later, when I started college in his city, he began taking me to dinner at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday—a restaurant with heavy maroon drapes and waiters who wore black bow ties with an air of weary dignity. I suspected these dinners cost more than he should have spent, but there was something both touching and slightly oppressive about his insistence on maintaining this connection, as if he were fulfilling some deathbed promise to Aunt Nell that I'd never been told about. I assumed he could afford it; after all, he lived in an apartment building with a doorman and wore suits that looked expensive in their subtle way. But sometimes I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new. There are some kinds of family duty that run deeper than affection, I suppose, though I never quite knew which one brought Ernie to that restaurant every other Sunday, in his good suit, precisely on time.

written_by_MFA033.Original: My mother had a bachelor cousin a good deal younger than her, who used to visit us on the farm every summer. He brought along his mother, Aunt Nell Botts. His own name was Ernie Botts. He was a tall, florid man with a good-natured expression, a big square face, and fair curly hair springing straight up from his forehead. His hands, his fingernails were as clean as soap itself; his hips were a little plump. My name for him—when he was not around—was Earnest Bottom. I had a mean tongue.But I meant no harm. Or hardly any harm.After Aunt Nell Botts died Ernie did not come to visit anymore, but he always sent a Christmas card.When I started college in the city where he lived, he began a custom of taking me out to dinner every other Sunday evening. He did this because I was a relative—it’s unlikely that he even considered whether we were suited to spending time together. He always took me to the same place, a restaurant called the Old Chelsea, which was on the second floor of a building, looking down on Dundas Street. It had velvet curtains, white tablecloths, little rose-shaded lamps on the tables. It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.

From then, Ernie and I had dinner every other Sunday, at a place called the Old Chelsea. I wasn’t sure why. I couldn’t tell if he had real fondness for me. His old habits of grooming were accompanied now by a certain formality of speech. I assumed his loyalty to the Old Chelsea, and to me, meant he could easily afford such luxuries.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts—Earnest Bottom, as I’d christened him in the foolish privacy of my head—was the clean and well-groomed sort of boy my mother admired.  He was always neat, pressed, and polite, the kind who’d never show up with grass stains or a ripped shirt.  Each summer, he’d arrive at our farm with his mother, Aunt Nell, a high-pitched echo of my mother’s pronouncements on how a young man ought to behave.  After Aunt Nell passed, the summer visits stopped, replaced by the steady arrival of Christmas cards—always signed “Ernie,” never the “Earnest Bottom” of my childhood.    Years later, when I found myself in his city for college, Ernie took it upon himself to take me out to dinner every other Sunday.  The Old Chelsea, the restaurant he chose, was the kind of place with heavy silverware and hushed conversations, the sort of place I figured Ernie frequented—though how a bachelor school teacher could afford it, I didn’t know.  Perhaps I’d underestimated a school teacher’s salary, or perhaps, like the old aunts I’d left back home, he’d scrimped and saved for the sake of appearances.  Ernie wasn’t much of a conversationalist, and I often found myself making idle chatter, filling the silences between his polite inquiries about my studies and his pronouncements on the weather.  I figured it was family duty that brought him, not any real desire for my company.  Still, there was something amusing about being seen in such a place with a man like Ernie—Earnest Bottom, the clean-cut boy turned proper bachelor.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Aunt Nell used to tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm every summer like he was an old handbag or umbrella. He never seemed to mind, smiling banally to show off his fantastic straight, white teeth. He was a clean boy, a good boy, so much so that in the privacy of my own mind, I called him Earnest Bottom. When Aunt Nell passed, there was no one to drag sweet Ernie around, so we stopped seeing him for a while. Mother made sure to send him Christmas cards every year, and I’d doodle him little flowers and rainbows on the back. After I was accepted into college, I wrote him a little note instead, telling him I’d be moving to his city. He wrote back saying we really ought to get dinner once I was settled. We did, and it morphed into an every-other-Sunday affair. Ernie would pick me up at my dorm and drive me to a charming little restaurant called the Old Chelsea. Ernie insisted on us ordering two appetizers each, a main course, dessert, and of course, an after-dinner coffee. The checks, when I managed to glimpse them, always made my eyes bug. But Ernie was a good person, and the elaborate dinners never seemed to me a desire to show off, but rather a way to remain a part of the family. If he could spend so confidently every other week, I presumed he was working one of those legitimate office jobs. He never did talk all that much about himself.

His hands, his fingernails were as clean as soap itself; his hips were a little plump. My name for him—when he was not around—was Earnest Bottom. I had a mean tongue.But I meant no harm. Or hardly any harm.After Aunt Nell Botts died Ernie did not come to visit anymore, but he always sent a Christmas card.When I started college in the city where he lived, he began a custom of taking me out to dinner every other Sunday evening. He did this because I was a relative—it’s unlikely that he even considered whether we were suited to spending time together. He always took me to the same place, a restaurant called the Old Chelsea, which was on the second floor of a building, looking down on Dundas Street. It had velvet curtains, white tablecloths, little rose-shaded lamps on the tables. It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts—Earnest Bottom, as I’d christened him in the foolish privacy of my head—was the clean and well-groomed sort of boy my mother admired.  He was always neat, pressed, and polite, the kind who’d never show up with grass stains or a ripped shirt.  Each summer, he’d arrive at our farm with his mother, Aunt Nell, a high-pitched echo of my mother’s pronouncements on how a young man ought to behave.  After Aunt Nell passed, the summer visits stopped, replaced by the steady arrival of Christmas cards—always signed “Ernie,” never the “Earnest Bottom” of my childhood.    Years later, when I found myself in his city for college, Ernie took it upon himself to take me out to dinner every other Sunday.  The Old Chelsea, the restaurant he chose, was the kind of place with heavy silverware and hushed conversations, the sort of place I figured Ernie frequented—though how a bachelor school teacher could afford it, I didn’t know.  Perhaps I’d underestimated a school teacher’s salary, or perhaps, like the old aunts I’d left back home, he’d scrimped and saved for the sake of appearances.  Ernie wasn’t much of a conversationalist, and I often found myself making idle chatter, filling the silences between his polite inquiries about my studies and his pronouncements on the weather.  I figured it was family duty that brought him, not any real desire for my company.  Still, there was something amusing about being seen in such a place with a man like Ernie—Earnest Bottom, the clean-cut boy turned proper bachelor.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Aunt Nell used to tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm every summer like he was an old handbag or umbrella. He never seemed to mind, smiling banally to show off his fantastic straight, white teeth. He was a clean boy, a good boy, so much so that in the privacy of my own mind, I called him Earnest Bottom. When Aunt Nell passed, there was no one to drag sweet Ernie around, so we stopped seeing him for a while. Mother made sure to send him Christmas cards every year, and I’d doodle him little flowers and rainbows on the back. After I was accepted into college, I wrote him a little note instead, telling him I’d be moving to his city. He wrote back saying we really ought to get dinner once I was settled. We did, and it morphed into an every-other-Sunday affair. Ernie would pick me up at my dorm and drive me to a charming little restaurant called the Old Chelsea. Ernie insisted on us ordering two appetizers each, a main course, dessert, and of course, an after-dinner coffee. The checks, when I managed to glimpse them, always made my eyes bug. But Ernie was a good person, and the elaborate dinners never seemed to me a desire to show off, but rather a way to remain a part of the family. If he could spend so confidently every other week, I presumed he was working one of those legitimate office jobs. He never did talk all that much about himself.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It is impossible to think of the Old Chelsea without thinking, too, of Earnest Bottom. His real name, of course, was Ernie Botts—my slightly younger and far more sophisticated cousin. We'd spent many summers together as children at my family's farm. Ernie was prim and manicured and always seemed to be dusting off his pants or scraping mud from the soles of his shoes. At Aunt Nell's funeral, he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers. He stopped coming to the farm after that, but we kept in touch through Christmas cards, which he always signed with a kind, personalized note. Our paths ran perpendicular again when I went to graduate school in his city. As soon as he heard I was in town, he locked me into his calendar for dinner every other Sunday. The Old Chelsea had an excellent fillet mignon, he told me, and it was true. The food offset the conversation, which was stale at best. Talk of work and school died out quickly, and I felt guilty talking about my social life—while I was making friends and had started going steady with a classmate, Ernie seemed to be suspended in self-imposed monkhood. Somehow, the bill always ended up in Ernie's hands. “It’s the least I can do,” he’d say, batting away the money I offered, and I couldn’t help but wonder what he thought he owed me.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: During those summers on the farm, Ernie Botts, who we’d mischievously dubbed “Earnest Bottom,” became a predictable part of the season, like the first crop of sweet corn or the relentless hum of cicadas. He was always impeccably groomed—his blond hair neatly combed, his fingernails somehow untouched by dirt, even after a day spent traipsing through the fields. He was good-natured in a way that set him apart from the brashness of other cousins who fought over fishing rods or snickered at Aunt Nell’s awkward manners. Ernie simply smiled and carried on, often humming quietly as he helped with chores or indulged my younger siblings by playing checkers on the front porch. When Aunt Nell passed away, his visits ended, replaced only by his dutiful Christmas cards that seemed to grow shorter with each year. By the time I moved to his city for college, he was a figure shrouded in distant nostalgia, though he reappeared with an almost rehearsed sincerity, treating me to dinners at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday. The crisp white napkins, the polite waitstaff, the gleaming wine glasses—it all seemed to mirror Ernie himself, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that these outings were more about obligation than genuine kinship. But still, I didn’t protest. His generosity, even if tinged with a faint remoteness, filled the silences left by years and miles, a duty performed with meticulous care and quiet resolve.

He was good-natured in a way that set him apart from the brashness of other cousins who fought over fishing rods or snickered at Aunt Nell’s awkward manners. Ernie simply smiled and carried on, often humming quietly as he helped with chores or indulged my younger siblings by playing checkers on the front porch. When Aunt Nell passed away, his visits ended, replaced only by his dutiful Christmas cards that seemed to grow shorter with each year. By the time I moved to his city for college, he was a figure shrouded in distant nostalgia, though he reappeared with an almost rehearsed sincerity, treating me to dinners at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday. The crisp white napkins, the polite waitstaff, the gleaming wine glasses—it all seemed to mirror Ernie himself, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that these outings were more about obligation than genuine kinship. But still, I didn’t protest. His generosity, even if tinged with a faint remoteness, filled the silences left by years and miles, a duty performed with meticulous care and quiet resolve.

written_by_MFA029.Original: My mother had a bachelor cousin a good deal younger than her, who used to visit us on the farm every summer. He brought along his mother, Aunt Nell Botts. His own name was Ernie Botts. He was a tall, florid man with a good-natured expression, a big square face, and fair curly hair springing straight up from his forehead. His hands, his fingernails were as clean as soap itself; his hips were a little plump. My name for him—when he was not around—was Earnest Bottom. I had a mean tongue.But I meant no harm. Or hardly any harm.After Aunt Nell Botts died Ernie did not come to visit anymore, but he always sent a Christmas card.When I started college in the city where he lived, he began a custom of taking me out to dinner every other Sunday evening. He did this because I was a relative—it’s unlikely that he even considered whether we were suited to spending time together. He always took me to the same place, a restaurant called the Old Chelsea, which was on the second floor of a building, looking down on Dundas Street. It had velvet curtains, white tablecloths, little rose-shaded lamps on the tables. It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: It is impossible to think of the Old Chelsea without thinking, too, of Earnest Bottom. His real name, of course, was Ernie Botts—my slightly younger and far more sophisticated cousin. We'd spent many summers together as children at my family's farm. Ernie was prim and manicured and always seemed to be dusting off his pants or scraping mud from the soles of his shoes. At Aunt Nell's funeral, he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers. He stopped coming to the farm after that, but we kept in touch through Christmas cards, which he always signed with a kind, personalized note. Our paths ran perpendicular again when I went to graduate school in his city. As soon as he heard I was in town, he locked me into his calendar for dinner every other Sunday. The Old Chelsea had an excellent fillet mignon, he told me, and it was true. The food offset the conversation, which was stale at best. Talk of work and school died out quickly, and I felt guilty talking about my social life—while I was making friends and had started going steady with a classmate, Ernie seemed to be suspended in self-imposed monkhood. Somehow, the bill always ended up in Ernie's hands. “It’s the least I can do,” he’d say, batting away the money I offered, and I couldn’t help but wonder what he thought he owed me.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: We are watched. Always watched, but never truly seen. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrol the corridors with their cattle prods held like scepters, symbols of their petty authority, though it's the Angels outside who hold the real power, with their guns and their untouchable distance. I've memorized the way they stand, these Angels, their backs military-straight against the concrete walls, their eyes hidden beneath the peaks of their caps. Sometimes I imagine their gaze following me, and I let my hips sway ever so slightly – an old habit from before, when such movements held currency. Now they're just muscle memory, like the way my hands still reach for a phone that isn't there, or my fingers itch for a cigarette I can't have. The other women do it too; I see them in the cafeteria, in the exercise yard, their bodies unconsciously remembering freedom. We're like cats in a cage, I think, practicing our hunting crouch though there's nothing left to hunt. At night, in our narrow beds, we whisper about making deals – our bodies for their help, as if we still owned these vessels we inhabit. As if flesh could buy freedom in a place where flesh is all we're reduced to. The routine grinds on: wake, pray, eat, walk, pray, sleep. The cold seeps in through the windows, but it's nothing compared to the chill that's settled in our bones. We are learning to fold ourselves smaller, to take up less space, to become invisible even as we're constantly observed. Yet somewhere, in the midnight hours when even Aunt Sara's footsteps fade, we dream of tomorrow, of a future that feels as distant and unreachable as the stars beyond our barred windows.

written_by_MFA029.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil.  But these desires are forbidden, locked away in the depths of our sterile existence. Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers.  We steal glances, share whispered secrets, and dream of a future beyond these walls.  Our bodies may be captive, but our minds remain free.In the dead of night, when the silence is broken only by the rhythmic hum of the surveillance cameras, I close my eyes and envision a world ablaze with color, a world where laughter rings out like music, a world where desires are not forbidden.  It is a world worth fighting for, a world worth dying for.And so we wait, with bated breath, for the moment when the chains will break, and we will emerge from the shadows, like butterflies from their chrysalises, ready to embrace the future, no matter how uncertain it may be.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.

Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers.  We steal glances, share whispered secrets, and dream of a future beyond these walls.  Our bodies may be captive, but our minds remain free.In the dead of night, when the silence is broken only by the rhythmic hum of the surveillance cameras, I close my eyes and envision a world ablaze with color, a world where laughter rings out like music, a world where desires are not forbidden.  It is a world worth fighting for, a world worth dying for.And so we wait, with bated breath, for the moment when the chains will break, and we will emerge from the shadows, like butterflies from their chrysalises, ready to embrace the future, no matter how uncertain it may be.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.
written_by_MFA004.Reason: Excerpt 2 is closer to the original passage in terms of voice and style. The flow of both issteady and grounded in the narrator's specific perspective and the writing in both is rhythmic and textured. They both also are just more effective and cohesive than 1 in telling the story.
written_by_MFA004.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The air here is brittle, like dried leaves crushed underfoot, and the fluorescent lights buzz with a monotony that drills into the skull. I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. They say we’re not to speak unless spoken to, but language has become a thing of eyes, of hands, of unspoken bargains, a subversive currency that Aunt Sara can’t see, no matter how sharp her gaze.When the bell rings, we file into formation, a line of bodies stripped of agency, like cattle awaiting slaughter. The air smells of antiseptic and faint decay, the institutional perfume of despair. Still, the future hums faintly, a promise just out of reach. Maybe tomorrow one of us will break through, touch the world beyond the fences. Maybe tomorrow the Angels will look back. Maybe tomorrow the tiles will finally add up to freedom.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.

I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne sits on the worn leather couch, her fingers absently tracing the cracked armrest while Connell stands by the window, his reflection fragmenting in the rain-spotted glass. The conversation hangs between them like something delicate and inevitable, the kind of moment that will later be dissected in therapy sessions or late-night emails. "I wouldn't have any of this without you," he says, and Marianne notices how he gestures vaguely at nothing in particular, at everything, at the literary magazines on the coffee table, at his MacBook with half-finished submissions to publishing houses. She thinks about how they've grown together, feeding off each other's neuroses and ambitions like some sort of symbiotic organism, each taking what they needed and giving what they could. The irony doesn't escape her - that their relationship, which started in whispered conversations in empty school corridors, had somehow shaped them into people who could write about love and loss in ways that made strangers feel seen. A notification lights up her phone: an email from her agent, or maybe just Deliveroo. She doesn't check. Instead, she watches Connell's hands, remembering how they used to nervously adjust his collar during their first readings together at literary festivals. Now they're steady as he explains why he has to leave, using words like 'growth' and 'space' that sound like they've been borrowed from a self-help podcast. The truth is, she's not the same person who needed his validation to feel real anymore. That girl, who used to check his online status compulsively and craft clever responses to his texts, seems like a character in someone else's story now. People change each other, she thinks, that's just what they do, like weather systems colliding and creating something new. She doesn't say this out loud. Instead, she says, "Okay," and watches his reflection blur further in the glass.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.

"I wouldn't have any of this without you," he says, and Marianne notices how he gestures vaguely at nothing in particular, at everything, at the literary magazines on the coffee table, at his MacBook with half-finished submissions to publishing houses. She thinks about how they've grown together, feeding off each other's neuroses and ambitions like some sort of symbiotic organism, each taking what they needed and giving what they could. The irony doesn't escape her - that their relationship, which started in whispered conversations in empty school corridors, had somehow shaped them into people who could write about love and loss in ways that made strangers feel seen. A notification lights up her phone: an email from her agent, or maybe just Deliveroo. She doesn't check. Instead, she watches Connell's hands, remembering how they used to nervously adjust his collar during their first readings together at literary festivals. Now they're steady as he explains why he has to leave, using words like 'growth' and 'space' that sound like they've been borrowed from a self-help podcast. The truth is, she's not the same person who needed his validation to feel real anymore. That girl, who used to check his online status compulsively and craft clever responses to his texts, seems like a character in someone else's story now. People change each other, she thinks, that's just what they do, like weather systems colliding and creating something new. She doesn't say this out loud. Instead, she says, "Okay," and watches his reflection blur further in the glass.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.
written_by_MFA008.Reason:
Excerpt 1 has distracting details that place it in the present (mentions of a MacBook, Deliveroo, etc.", while Excerpt 2 and the Original have a timelessness to them.
Excerpt 2 and the original both reference plants in a pot of soil. They also both open with Connell's thoughts rather than Marianne.
written_by_MFA008.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. And Marianne herself, she would be another person completely. Would she ever have been happy? And what kind of happiness might it have been? All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room, taking certain unlikely positions. But in the end she has done something for him, she’s made a new life possible, and she can always feel good about that. I'd miss you too much, he says. I’d be sick, honestly. At first. But it would get better. They sit in silence now, Marianne moving the brush methodically through her hair, feeling for knots and slowly, patiently untangling them. There's no point in being impatient anymore. You know I love you, says Connell. I'm never going to feel the same way for someone else. She nods, okay. He's telling the truth. To be honest, I don’t know what to do, he says. Say you want me to stay and I will. She closes her eyes. He probably won’t come back, she thinks. Or he will, differently. What they have now they can never have back again. But for her the pain of loneliness will be nothing to the pain that she used to feel, of being unworthy. He brought her goodness like a gift and now it belongs to her. Meanwhile his life opens out before him in all directions at once. They’ve done a lot of good for each other. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Connell said it quietly, his voice catching somewhere in his throat: I wouldn’t have anything without you, you know. Marianne, sitting opposite him, didn’t reply immediately. Her hands were on the table, palms flat, as though grounding herself against the possibility that this was really happening. She thought about the moments when they had each shaped the other in ways small and monumental, like two plants twisting together in the same patch of soil, entwined but separate, their growths inescapably altered by proximity. Connell exhaled sharply, leaning back in his chair as if retreating from his own words. “You’ve done more for me than anyone,” he added, not looking at her now. Marianne felt her chest tighten. She understood what he meant, of course—she’d spent years reflecting on the way they fit together, how they’d softened each other's sharp edges and inadvertently revealed their deepest flaws. And yet, sitting here, she also knew that time had shifted something irreparably between them. He could leave now, and she would still wake up tomorrow. She would still exist. For a long time, she hadn’t believed that. She pressed her fingers against the wood of the table, cool and solid under her touch. “You’ve done a lot for me, too,” she said finally, her voice almost neutral. She thought about how he’d pulled her back from the darker edges of herself, the places where loneliness masqueraded as unworthiness. But that was a long time ago, she thought now, and it wasn’t the same. “People change each other, Connell,” she said. “And then they keep changing, even after.” He nodded slightly, his jaw tense. Neither of them moved to close the distance between their chairs, the space heavy with what neither of them could bring themselves to say. Life would go on, she knew. And she would go on with it.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The glass partition reflected my spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn, as we sat at the group table near the kitchen. My father's hands, roughened by work, rested uneasily on the paper placemat while we waited, ignored by the waiters who glided past with studied indifference. At the next table, a girl my age lounged with casual elegance, her summer-bronzed skin gleaming against a crisp white blouse. She spooned yogurt—a food I had never tasted—with the natural grace of someone who had always known its existence. Her father, well-dressed and at ease, gestured expressively as he spoke to her. They had ordered à la carte, their plates arranged with careful precision by attentive staff. When our fixed-price meals finally arrived, the mashed potatoes sat in a grayish heap, unmolded from some industrial container. My father ate in silence, his shoulders tense, his fork scraping the institutional plate. For days afterward, he would mutter about the "pig slop" they had served us, each repetition of the phrase carrying the accumulated weight of a lifetime of similar humiliations. I understood then that the restaurant had sorted us, placed us in our proper social category—the cheap seats, the hurried service, the institutional food. We belonged to the world of fixed-price menus and group tables, while others inhabited the realm of individual choice, of yogurt and carefully plated dishes, of being seen and served with deference.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement.  At our table, a shared expanse with strangers, the service was a reluctant dance of neglect.  In contrast, a few tables away, a tanned teenage girl, radiating an aura of effortless confidence, shared an intimate meal with an older man.  Her laughter, light and carefree, bounced off the gilded mirrors, mocking my own constrained stillness.Her spoon, a silver arc, delivered a dollop of yogurt to her lips—a food so exotic, it was a whisper from another world.  My gaze drifted back to my plate, the food suddenly as bland as the pity I felt for myself. written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: It was Saint Patrick's Day when I watched my mother die, though there was nothing lucky about that bitter-bright morning. The sun bounced off snow banks outside her window, creating a cruel sparkle that seemed to mock the dimming light within. A cup of green Jell-O sat untouched on her bedside table – some nurse's attempt at festivity that now seemed obscene in its cheerfulness. My mother's eyes were the color of forgotten summers, a blue so startling against her pallid skin that it made my chest ache. They remained open, fixed on something I couldn't see, something beyond the sterile hospital walls and my desperate presence beside her. I watched death move through her like smoke through a burning house, slow and inevitable, claiming each room until nothing remained but ash. Those eyes – I saw everything in them. First came the bitterness, sharp as broken glass, then confusion that softened her face into something childlike, and finally, a quiet courage that broke my heart and rebuilt it in the same moment. The blue of her irises burned like pilot lights, struggling to stay lit even as the rest of her failed. Even now, I can close my eyes and see that color, that last fierce flag of life she waved, refusing to surrender until the very end. How wild it was, to watch someone both fight and accept their fate in the same endless moment.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: The winter light was dimming, Saint Patrick’s Day fading into a muted gray. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick’s Day, though there was no room for festivity in the hospital room where my mother lay suspended between this life and the next. Outside, the sunlight refracted sharply off the icy snow, casting a dazzling brilliance that mocked the stillness inside. Beside her, a bowl of green Jell-O sat untouched, its lurid color out of place in the solemnity of the moment. My mother’s eyes, blue and unyielding, remained open, vivid against the pallor of her skin and the muted sterility of the room. She was there but not there—unresponsive, yet undeniably present. I watched her, saw her dying like a fire slowly extinguishing into smoke, the embers of her vitality winking out one by one. Her eyes, once fierce with bitterness, shifted to bewilderment, and finally, to a quiet, unspoken heroism. They were the eyes of someone who clung to life even as it slipped from her grasp, a desperate yearning embedded in that piercing blue. The blue of her eyes became my lodestar, a symbol of her fight, her grace, her inevitability. And as I held her hand, I knew that when she closed those eyes for the last time, they would remain etched in me forever, as luminous as the snow outside.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
