written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In that sea-green building which stood like a tired sentinel near Elliot's Beach (where young lovers would soon gather with their smartphones and their dreams, as predictable as the tide), there lived two old men whose synchronicity of existence would have alarmed them had they ever bothered to notice it—but they never did, for such is the peculiar blindness that affects those who are bound together by the invisible threads of fate. The fourth floor (ah, but was it really the fourth? for in this particular building the ground floor was called the first, in the American way, causing endless confusion among visitors and delivery men alike) housed Senior and Junior, names that contained their own little joke, since Junior was himself no spring chicken, and Senior was so ancient that some believed he had witnessed the departure of the British Raj with his own rheumy eyes. Every morning, as predictable as the muezzin's call to prayer that floated across the neighborhood like a ghost's lament, mixing with the timpani of temple bells and the cheerful vulgarity of Tamil film songs blaring from auto-rickshaws, the two men would emerge onto their respective verandas at precisely the same moment, like mechanical figures in some elaborate timepiece. The morning air arrived thick with stories: the dark, intense aroma of filter coffee from the houses below, where young IT professionals fueled themselves for their days in air-conditioned offices; the shouts of children in pressed uniforms hurrying to school, their watches synchronized to their mothers' anxieties; the eternal complaint of crows who had seen it all before and were distinctly unimpressed. The heat rose from the streets like a malevolent spirit, distorting the reality of things, so that the two old men, standing on their respective verandas with their respective cups of tea, might have been mirror images of each other, or perhaps the same man caught in two different moments of time, or even (though they would have scoffed at such fancy) two aspects of the same soul, divided at birth and now slowly, incrementally, moving toward an inevitable reunion, like two drops of water on a window pane, drawn together by forces beyond their comprehension or control.

written_by_MFA025.Original: The day that Junior fell down began like any other day: the explosion of heat rippling the air, the trumpeting sunlight, the traffic’s tidal surges, the prayer chants in the distance, the cheap film music rising from the floor below, the loud pelvic thrusts of an 'item number' dancing across a neighbor’s TV, a child’s cry, a mother’s rebuke, unexplained laughter, scarlet expectorations, bicycles, the newly plaited hair of schoolgirls, the smell of strong sweet coffee, a green wing flashing in a tree. Senior and Junior, two very old men, opened their eyes in their bedrooms on the fourth floor of a sea-green building on a leafy lane, just out of sight of Elliot’s Beach, where, that evening, the young would congregate, as they always did, to perform the rites of youth, not far from the village of the fisherfolk, who had no time for such frivolity. The two men, unhurried and deliberate, bore witness to it all—custodians of a pace the world had long since abandoned.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.

written_by_MFA030.Original: Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in from the forest and had used the awkward, angular objects they had found, walls, doors, windows, furniture, to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut. Within drawing-rooms they had built shelters; they had raised roofs on verandah half-walls. Fires burned on pieces of corrugated iron; bricks were the cooking stones. On the sidewalks grass had grown around rubbish from the houses, things that couldn’t be used and had been thrown out: cracked squares of picture glass, fragments of upholstered chairs, mattresses that had been disembowelled for their springs, books and magazines whose pages had stuck together in solid, crinkled pads. Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. This resort hadn’t been built for tourists in Africa; it had been created by people who thought they had come to Africa to stay, and looked in a resort for a version of the things of home: a park, a pier, a waterside promenade. Now, after the troubles across the lake, after independence and the property scare, after the army mutiny, after the white exodus South and the Asian deportations, after all these deaths, the resort no longer had a function.

written_by_MFA030.Original: Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in from the forest and had used the awkward, angular objects they had found, walls, doors, windows, furniture, to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut. Within drawing-rooms they had built shelters; they had raised roofs on verandah half-walls. Fires burned on pieces of corrugated iron; bricks were the cooking stones. On the sidewalks grass had grown around rubbish from the houses, things that couldn’t be used and had been thrown out: cracked squares of picture glass, fragments of upholstered chairs, mattresses that had been disembowelled for their springs, books and magazines whose pages had stuck together in solid, crinkled pads. Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. This resort hadn’t been built for tourists in Africa; it had been created by people who thought they had come to Africa to stay, and looked in a resort for a version of the things of home: a park, a pier, a waterside promenade. Now, after the troubles across the lake, after independence and the property scare, after the army mutiny, after the white exodus South and the Asian deportations, after all these deaths, the resort no longer had a function.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: The once-vibrant resort now stood in a state of decay, a stark reminder of the societal shifts that had swept through the region.  The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: I am having to rush at this point, but think excerpt 2 offers a response closer to the original in both voice and style than excerpt 1. It talks of the recollection in the same tone and feeling. Excerpt 1 offers a more vivid story and chilling ending than the other.
written_by_MFA010.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: That Christmas morning, my father handed me an envelope, thick with cash, along with a brochure for Disney World, its glossy pages showcasing artificial castles and choreographed joy. "We leave next week," he said, his voice carrying that familiar mixture of authority and hesitation that had marked our relationship since my mother's death. I watched Chitra in the kitchen, methodically preparing tea, her movements precise and deliberate, like someone navigating through a space that wasn't quite her own. Through the window, I could see Rupa and Piu in the backyard, their matching winter coats making them look like mirror images as they built a lopsided snowman. I manufactured an excuse about a winter session course, watching their small shoulders slump when my father relayed the news. The girls had wanted to share their Disney princess fantasies with their older sister, not understanding that I was a relic of a different fairy tale, one that had ended with my mother's last breath in a stark hospital room. Later, as I folded the crisp bills and tucked them into my wallet, I caught Chitra's fleeting glance – a look of relief poorly disguised as sympathy. My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence. I recognized then that we were all performing our roles: they as the new family looking forward, me as the keeper of memories, standing still in a house that held too many ghosts.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Excerpt 1 seems clsoer to the original, because the focus remains fixed on the narrator's negative feelings toward his father and his new companion ("Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday"), whereas, in Excerpt 2, it ends with an exploration of his father's attitudes ("My father busied himself with travel arrangements, his enthusiasm slightly too pronounced, betraying the comfort he found in my absence"), followed by the narrator's extensive ruminations about his own feelings (of "standing still in a house that held too many ghosts").
written_by_MFA010.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The crisp bill tucked into my palm felt unfamiliar, the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface.  My father, in his crisp suit and polished shoes, stood before me, the scent of his new life – a blend of unfamiliar spices and expensive cologne – clinging to him like a second skin.  His words echoed in the sterile expanse of the hotel room, an invitation to a world I no longer recognized.  "Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench.  "Just you, me, Chitra, and the girls."My mouth formed the words of refusal, a practiced excuse about school and looming deadlines, but the lie tasted like ash.  In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion.  They were a part of him, just as I was a part of her, the ghost that lingered in the corners of our lives.Later, as I stood on the balcony, the city lights blurring into a sea of neon, I felt a strange sense of relief emanating from them.  They wanted to move on, to build something new, untainted by the past.  And I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a love lost, was a burden they no longer wished to carry.  The distance between us was a physical manifestation of the years that had passed, the laughter and tears that had reshaped our lives.  It was a gulf that could not be bridged, a chasm carved by grief and the relentless march of time.

My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. But he continued explaining, and all the while his eyes remained trained on his girls, who were prostrate under the tree. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. Not a ticket on a red-eye to Orlando, not a room at the same overpriced hotel or a paid-for day pass—-it was simply these words: “And of course, you can join us at Disney World, if you would like.” From the kitchen, Chitra added her ringing voice to his: “Only if you want! There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The crisp bill tucked into my palm felt unfamiliar, the weight of its promise as foreign as the characters etched onto its surface.  My father, in his crisp suit and polished shoes, stood before me, the scent of his new life – a blend of unfamiliar spices and expensive cologne – clinging to him like a second skin.  His words echoed in the sterile expanse of the hotel room, an invitation to a world I no longer recognized.  "Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench.  "Just you, me, Chitra, and the girls."My mouth formed the words of refusal, a practiced excuse about school and looming deadlines, but the lie tasted like ash.  In their eyes, the disappointment was a tangible thing, sharp and cutting.  Rupa's lower lip trembled, a mirror of the tremor in my own heart.  Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion.  They were a part of him, just as I was a part of her, the ghost that lingered in the corners of our lives.Later, as I stood on the balcony, the city lights blurring into a sea of neon, I felt a strange sense of relief emanating from them.  They wanted to move on, to build something new, untainted by the past.  And I, the keeper of memories, the guardian of a love lost, was a burden they no longer wished to carry.  The distance between us was a physical manifestation of the years that had passed, the laughter and tears that had reshaped our lives.  It was a gulf that could not be bridged, a chasm carved by grief and the relentless march of time.

Excerpt 2 is very dramatic and descriptive and slightly moves away from the original story. Excerpt 1 maintains the same overall impression of the original.

"Disney World," he'd said, the syllables rolling off his tongue with a practiced ease that made my stomach clench. Piu, ever the stoic, simply stared, her dark eyes pools of confusion. The girls are excited.” Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words. “I can’t,” I said, the excuse tumbling out. “There’s a project—due after break.” The lie felt hollow, but I let it stand. Chitra placed a dish of fruit on the table, her movements brisk, her expression neutral, as if my refusal required no comment. My father leaned back, resigned, a faint relief softening the tension in his jaw. I sensed how the trip would be easier without me—how my presence reminded them of another family, one they had worked hard to unwrite. Later, when I passed the girls in the hallway, they whispered in hurried tones, their laughter abruptly silenced when I appeared. I thought of my mother, the spaces she had filled now occupied by others, and felt caught between loyalties, between memory and their momentum forward. Outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: I think the second one is slightly better written. However, these are both very similar to the original in my opinion, so I think either would work well with the original text. They employ the same writing style and both seem coherent and naturally flow about the same and are both effective, but I would choose the second one just bit the narrowest of margins.
written_by_MFA016.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Standing in that vast field, with discarded papers and empty bottles tumbling past in the wind, I found myself giving in—just briefly—to an old habit of fantasy. Perhaps it wasn't entirely sensible, but I allowed myself to imagine this desolate spot as a kind of gathering place, where all the things one has lost might eventually wash up. The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

Excerpt 2 has a very different voice and style from the original excerpt. written_by_MFA015.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

The thought came to me quite naturally, watching a plastic bag rise and fall in the gusting wind, that this could be where everything drifts to: old photographs, missed opportunities, unspoken words—all the things one somehow let slip away. And then, as though my mind had been waiting for just such a moment, I saw him—or rather, allowed myself to see him—Tommy, emerging from the hazy horizon, his hand raised in that familiar wave of his. But of course, one can't afford to let such fancies go too far. Even as I felt the tears sliding down my cheeks, I maintained a certain composure, the way one must. After all, what sense was there in pursuing these rather foolish thoughts? So I stood there a moment longer, letting the wind dry my face, before turning back to my car. There were things to be done, and one simply had to get on with them.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: The way excerpt 2 describes their surroundings and their feelings towards Tommy and the memories of him sound more similar to the original. The tone of voice sounds similar and nostalgic and the flow of the text is much more similar to the original compared to excerpt 1 which is less flowing
written_by_MFA015.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The wind whipped around me, tearing at my clothes and sending the scattered debris dancing across the desolate expanse of the field.  It was a place of stark beauty, where the horizon stretched out like an endless ribbon, and the sky, a vast canvas of swirling greys and blues, mirrored the turmoil within my own heart.For a moment, I allowed myself to be swept away by a fantasy, to imagine that all the things I'd lost in life had somehow washed up here, deposited by the relentless tide of time.  And in that fantastical vision, I saw him, Tommy, his familiar figure emerging from the distant haze, a gentle smile gracing his lips as he waved to me.But I stopped the fantasy before it could take root, before it could weave its way into the fabric of my reality.  The tears came, but I held them back, refusing to let them spill over.  There was a quiet acceptance in that moment, a recognition of the finality of loss. After a while, I turned and walked back to my car, leaving behind the windswept field and the echoes of my fantasy.  The road ahead stretched out before me, a path that I would travel alone, but with a newfound sense of peace.  The world was still there, waiting for me, and life, in all its complexity and beauty, would go on.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. Or, more precisely, an image of Tommy, his left hand lifted in a wave. But I didn't let the fantasy go too far. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. I wasn’t crying hard or soft—in fact, after a while I wasn’t crying at all, and then I went to my car. Things couldn’t come back, I knew. They could only decompose.

And in that fantastical vision, I saw him, Tommy, his familiar figure emerging from the distant haze, a gentle smile gracing his lips as he waved to me.But I stopped the fantasy before it could take root, before it could weave its way into the fabric of my reality.  The tears came, but I held them back, refusing to let them spill over.  There was a quiet acceptance in that moment, a recognition of the finality of loss. After a while, I turned and walked back to my car, leaving behind the windswept field and the echoes of my fantasy.  The road ahead stretched out before me, a path that I would travel alone, but with a newfound sense of peace.  The world was still there, waiting for me, and life, in all its complexity and beauty, would go on.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: The first excerpt is more like the original because it tells the story by getting straight to the point and describes the scene in a very simple way that is clear and easy to read without much flourish. The second excerpt has a lot of extra detail that exaggerates or completely changes the feel of the story such as saying and in that fantastical vision... rather than simply stating that for a moment I imagined or calling it a fantasy, and the original saying that I half-closed my eyes and imagined.
written_by_MFA007.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. Or, more precisely, an image of Tommy, his left hand lifted in a wave. But I didn't let the fantasy go too far. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. I wasn’t crying hard or soft—in fact, after a while I wasn’t crying at all, and then I went to my car. Things couldn’t come back, I knew. They could only decompose.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Samad sat there, his fingers drumming against the pub table, each tap a tiny rebellion against the polished oak surface that had witnessed centuries of English contemplation. "You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." He was not sure why he was telling this to the waiter, because he couldn't tell if it was real ash or maybe just little crumbs from the tea itself."Oh dear, I'm sorry sir. I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.

"You see," he began, his voice carrying that particular tone of a man who has rehearsed his grievances in the mirror, "this country, this England, it's like one of those fancy department stores where they let you browse but never expect you to buy anything." He paused, taking a theatrical sip of his whiskey—a drink he'd adopted precisely because it made him feel like a fraud. "My son—the one who wears those ridiculous pinstripe suits—he thinks he's fooled them all. Barrister this, Westminster that. But they see through it, oh yes, they do. And the other one?" He laughed, but it was the kind of laugh that carries more warning than humor. "He's gone and done exactly what they feared we all would. Turned himself into their worst nightmare, hasn't he? A proper fundamentalist. Both of them are just different sides of the same bloody English pound." Irie, who had been watching this performance with the patient attention of someone who had seen it many times before, interjected softly, "Oh, that's not true, surely." But Samad was already racing ahead, carried by the momentum of his discontent. "When I came here, I thought—just a few years, make some money, go home a success. Instead?" He spread his arms wide, encompassing the pub, the street outside, the whole of London, "Instead, I've become this strange creature who belongs nowhere. Not here, where they 'tolerate' us—" he spat the word like a pip from a bitter fruit—"and not there, where I'm now too English to fit in. Tell me, what is a birthplace anyway? A cosmic accident? A life sentence? Or just another pretty lie we tell ourselves while we're busy being lost?" He turned back to his whiskey, his reflection in the mirror behind the bar showing a man caught between what he was and what he had become, between where he was from and where he had landed—a man trapped in the hyphen of British-Bengali identity.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: "There is a speck of ash at the bottom of this cup of tea." That's what they used to tell me when I first arrived. Before my voice began to sound like theirs, before I knew what a three-piece coat was, before I knew how to take the trolley.And now, he insists on talking to me as if I'm just one of them. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? To join the ranks of those torn, of those divided? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Samad leaned back, fingers tightening around the stem of his glass, watching the amber liquid swirl, gathering his thoughts like a man recalling a half-forgotten dream. "You know, Irie, I did not come here to stay," he began, with the kind of dramatic pause he enjoyed, as if delivering some great revelation. "No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."

"No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.

written_by_MFA008.Original: "There are no words. The one I send home comes out a pukka Englishman, white suited, silly wig lawyer. The one I keep here is fully paid-up green bow-tie-wearing fundamentalist terrorist. I sometimes wonder why I bother," said Samad bitterly, betraying the English inflections of twenty years in the country, "I really do. These days, it feels to me like you make a devil’s pact when you walk into this country. You hand over your passport at the check-in, you get stamped, you want to make a little money, get yourself started. but you mean to go back! Who would want to stay? Cold, wet, miserable; terrible food, dreadful newspapers — who would want to stay? In a place where you are never welcomed, only tolerated. Just tolerated. Like you are an animal finally house-trained. Who would want to stay? But you have made a devil’s pact... it drags you in and suddenly you are unsuitable to return, your children are unrecognizable, you belong nowhere." "Oh, that’s not true, surely." "And then you begin to give up the very idea of belonging. Suddenly this thing, this belonging, it seems like some long, dirty lie... and I begin to believe that birthplaces are accidents, that everything is an accident. But if you believe that, where do you go? What do you do? What does anything matter?"

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."

"No. It was meant to be temporary, a short stint, a little adventure before going home, but then—ah, then!—this country does something to you, something insidious. You come thinking you are a visitor, and before you know it, you have children who speak back to you in accents you don’t recognize, who call you old-fashioned, who think the way you eat, the way you pray, the way you exist is some sort of historical relic." He sighed, gesturing vaguely at the street outside. "One son, a lawyer. A proper pukka Englishman, with his nice suits and his nice house and his nice friends who politely pretend not to see the color of his skin. The other?" A mirthless laugh. "A warrior. A martyr. At least that’s what he believes. This place—it stretches you, splits you down the middle. And you, you keep asking yourself: where do I belong? Here? There? Nowhere?" He shook his head. "They tolerate us, Irie. Tolerate. Like a mild skin condition." Irie frowned. "Oh, that’s not true, surely." Samad just smiled, a tired, knowing thing.

written_by_MFA008.Original: "There are no words. The one I send home comes out a pukka Englishman, white suited, silly wig lawyer. The one I keep here is fully paid-up green bow-tie-wearing fundamentalist terrorist. I sometimes wonder why I bother," said Samad bitterly, betraying the English inflections of twenty years in the country, "I really do. These days, it feels to me like you make a devil’s pact when you walk into this country. You hand over your passport at the check-in, you get stamped, you want to make a little money, get yourself started. but you mean to go back! Who would want to stay? Cold, wet, miserable; terrible food, dreadful newspapers — who would want to stay? In a place where you are never welcomed, only tolerated. Just tolerated. Like you are an animal finally house-trained. Who would want to stay? But you have made a devil’s pact... it drags you in and suddenly you are unsuitable to return, your children are unrecognizable, you belong nowhere." "Oh, that’s not true, surely." "And then you begin to give up the very idea of belonging. Suddenly this thing, this belonging, it seems like some long, dirty lie... and I begin to believe that birthplaces are accidents, that everything is an accident. But if you believe that, where do you go? What do you do? What does anything matter?"

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: "If I could tell my own father about this!" cried Samad. "One son, with his marmite on toast and his football games. The other, a downright fundamentalist! More Bengali than I ever was. What would he have done, my father, if he could see me now? He would have said, It serves you right, Samad. That is what you get for going somewhere you are only tolerated." Samad paused and took a long sip of his tea. "Oh, Irie," he continued. "If I’d known that England was the way that it is. A place where we are merely tolerated. A place where belonging and not belonging both feel like a trap. Was it not pure foolishness, then, to come here? Not sometimes, but every single day, I know it was a mistake. We should have stayed put. What didn’t we stay put?” Irie shook her head. “That is not true, surely, Samad,” she said. “It’s England. It’s what we have always wanted. We dreamed of this place all our lives." "We dreamed of a version of this place, certainly," said Samad. "Truthfully, I don’t know what I believe anymore. I thought I knew what it meant to be born somewhere. But now? What does it matter where you are born? How can you belong anywhere if you feel... adrift. Every day. Completely adrift."

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: She sat across from Jean-Marc on the white-washed deck of the seaside restaurant, surrounded by an almost aggressive whiteness that seemed to mock the complexity of her emotions. The white tables, the white lampposts, even the moon hanging above the sea appeared to her as fragments of some cosmic unity she could never quite grasp. What puzzled her was not the nostalgia itself—that familiar heaviness in the chest that accompanies all human existence—but rather its peculiar timing. How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? Jean-Marc, with that subtle wisdom that occasionally visits lovers, understood that nostalgia is less about the past than about the terrifying possibility of future absence. It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. Then, like an uninvited guest at a funeral, came a thought of her dead child, followed by something even more unsettling: a sudden, inexplicable happiness. She felt ashamed of this happiness, as if she had committed an act of betrayal against grief itself. But who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions? We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. They come and go as they please, these emotions, paying no attention to the carefully arranged furniture of our convictions.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The whiteness of the drapes and tablecloth invoked in her the uneasy feeling of one blank canvas. Perhaps, there was an absence she wanted to forget. Her former husband had taken her to such seaside restaurants. But it wasn’t the absence of captured life that stirred in her some unrest but the anticipation of life, of color becoming, the canvas waiting. Even in colorful pockets of her vision–out the deck window to the yellow lampposts and dark ocean–it all bathed in the moon’s white glow. Opaque, the blurred background of a photograph. Yes, a photo, something calling back something that had been. And what of her life now? Why did now pass her as every prior moment had, leaving a feeling, for feelings to be the dropped breadcrumbs of life in its constant evasion? She was struck by an intense nostalgia for Jean-Marc.But how can one feel nostalgia for something — or someone — who sits merely an arm's length away?“Perhaps it’s the grief,” Jean-Marc said. “Your mind is preparing you for loss. Is it not easier to wrap these memories in a protective cloak of nostalgia?”If it was all for impending loss, then her mind was well acquainted. But it wasn’t grief she felt when she thought of her son. She imagined him swinging around the pole of a lamppost. Like breadcrumbs, she happened upon joy in the world’s dark vast woods. Feelings were given, never made. Her child was dead. Her husband was gone. Jean-Marc would one day be gone. And yet.

written_by_MFA003.Original: Much later, after she had left her husband and lived several years with Jean-Marc, she was at the seashore one day: they were dining outdoors, on a wooden deck over the water; she retains an intense memory of whiteness: the deck, the tables, the chairs, the tablecloths, everything was white, the lampposts were painted white and the bulbs beamed a white light against the summer sky, not yet dark, where the moon, itself white too, was whitening everything around them. And in this bath of white she was struck by a feeling of unbearable nostalgia for Jean-Marc. Nostalgia? How could she feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her? How can you suffer from the absence of a person who is present? (Jean-Marc knew how to answer that: you can suffer nostalgia in the presence of the beloved if you glimpse a future where the beloved is no more; if the beloved’s death is, invisibly, already present.) During that moment of strange nostalgia at the seaside, she suddenly thought of her dead child, and a wave of happiness flooded over her. Soon she would be frightened by this feeling. But no one can do a thing about feelings, they exist and there’s no way to censor them. We can reproach ourselves for some action, for a remark, but not for a feeling, quite simply because we have no control at all over it.

She thought the feeling meant: life will never get better than this. The future was her and Jean-Marc, together, but older, and recovered from the mania of fresh love, or perhaps not together at all. But how is it apprpropriate to feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her ? (Jean-Marc however had the answer: the more intensely we love someone in the present, the more we grieve their inevitable absence in some imagined future.) But she did not think that was what she meant at all! The mention of death made her think of the child. The child, forever a child, existing without complication in her death. The solidity of this shot her through with pure happiness. She felt afraid; she clasped her hands together in her lap and said nothing more. How easy it is to reign in our words and actions! But then there is always feeling, loping around like an untrained dog inside all of us, aware of how much we long to leash it.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The restaurant, awash in the starkness of white – the deck, the table, the lampposts, and even the moon, an orb of paleness in the sky, seemed to mirror the landscape of her emotions.  She was there with Jean-Marc, yet a wave of nostalgia, so intense, so profound, washed over her.  It was a peculiar sensation, this yearning for the past, when the object of her longing was right there beside her.  Jean-Marc, with the uncanny ability to read the intricate map of her heart, understood.  Such nostalgia, he explained, often veiled a deeper fear – the fear of losing a loved one, of a future where they were no longer present. And then, her thoughts drifted to her child, the one she had lost, a wound that had never fully healed.  In that moment, a flicker of happiness, as unexpected as a summer storm, surprised her.  The happiness was fleeting, replaced by a wave of fear at having experienced such a sensation.  It was as if emotions, like wayward children, refused to be tamed, to be told what to feel, when to feel.  We may choose our actions, our words, but feelings, those elusive specters, held sway over the uncharted territories of the heart.  They were the uninvited guests who barged in, the rebels who defied reason, the free spirits who danced to their own tune.

written_by_MFA006.Original: Much later, after she had left her husband and lived several years with Jean-Marc, she was at the seashore one day: they were dining outdoors, on a wooden deck over the water; she retains an intense memory of whiteness: the deck, the tables, the chairs, the tablecloths, everything was white, the lampposts were painted white and the bulbs beamed a white light against the summer sky, not yet dark, where the moon, itself white too, was whitening everything around them. And in this bath of white she was struck by a feeling of unbearable nostalgia for Jean-Marc. Nostalgia? How could she feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her? How can you suffer from the absence of a person who is present? (Jean-Marc knew how to answer that: you can suffer nostalgia in the presence of the beloved if you glimpse a future where the beloved is no more; if the beloved’s death is, invisibly, already present.) During that moment of strange nostalgia at the seaside, she suddenly thought of her dead child, and a wave of happiness flooded over her. Soon she would be frightened by this feeling. But no one can do a thing about feelings, they exist and there’s no way to censor them. We can reproach ourselves for some action, for a remark, but not for a feeling, quite simply because we have no control at all over it.

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: She sat across from Jean-Marc at the seaside restaurant, her fingers tracing invisible patterns on the white linen tablecloth, as if trying to anchor herself amidst the overwhelming brightness surrounding them. The deck stretched out, pale and gleaming, the lampposts shimmered like ghostly sentinels, and the moon hung low, casting an iridescent glow that seemed to swallow every color except white. The air was still, suffused with the faint, rhythmic whispers of the tide. Jean-Marc watched her, his expression serene yet attentive, as if he could read the kaleidoscope of emotions dancing behind her eyes. She felt a paradoxical pang of nostalgia—sharp and bittersweet—as though mourning something lost, though everything she cherished sat mere inches away. It puzzled her, this longing, this melancholy wrapped in an inexplicable happiness. Was it the memory of her deceased child, flitting unbidden into her mind like a shadow across the moonlight? Or was it the fear of losing Jean-Marc, his presence so vital it seemed like a delicate thread connecting her to the world? She smiled suddenly, a fleeting expression of joy so pure it frightened her. Jean-Marc reached for her hand, silently acknowledging the fragile beauty of her emotion. In that luminous moment, it struck her: we are masters of our actions, perhaps even of our words, but not of our feelings, those wild, untamed creatures that move within us, defying reason and will.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? She had left him because she wanted to; to be with the man she loved. The man sitting across from her now, handsome in a white button-down shirt. It suddenly struck her that everything in the seaside restaurant was white: the deck, the table, the lampposts. Even the moon, stark and full, shone unbearably white tonight. Jean-Marc asked: "What is the matter with you, my dear? You are so quiet tonight." "Nothing really," she said, knowing it was a lie. Something was wrong, but she could not put that something into words. It was a strange yet acute longing for what was already hers, sitting right there in front of her. Jean-Marc, feeling the melancholy in the air, said: "Nostalgia comes from the fear of losing someone and imagining life without them." She thought of her child, the only person she had truly lost. The memory struck her with unexpected happiness, followed immediately by fear. What did it mean to feel sadness at dinner with her lover but happiness thinking of her dead child? Was there something wrong with her? Was she a bad mother, a bad person? Not according to Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume had argued emotions were natural and involuntary. While we could control our actions, we could never control our feelings.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti. Like a monk devoted to a peculiar religion, I wandered through foreign grocery stores, filling my basket with olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world. The specialty shop owner—a thin man with circular glasses who looked like he could speak to cats—sold me a deep blue pot that seemed bottomless and a kitchen timer that ticked with the precision of a heartbeat. Strange how such ordinary objects can suddenly feel magical, as if they've crossed over from a parallel universe where pasta is a sacred thing. In my small apartment, which felt more like a submarine than a living space, I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars. The steam would rise and fog my windows, creating a barrier between my spaghetti sanctuary and the outside world. I never invited anyone to these meals—somehow, I knew this was a ritual meant for solitude, like writing poetry at midnight or counting clouds. Every Sunday, I'd prepare the same meal: spaghetti swimming in sauce that I'd cooked for exactly twenty-seven minutes, a green salad that seemed to whisper ancient mysteries, and tea that tasted of distant memories. The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.
