written_by_MFA015.Original: I went to a cooking specialty store and bought a kitchen timer and a huge aluminum pot, big enough to bathe a German shepherd in, then went around to all the supermarkets that catered to foreigners, gathering an assortment of odd-sounding spices. I picked up a pasta cookbook at the bookstore, and bought tomatoes by the dozen. I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man. Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week

I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1's style sticks more closely to the original. Excerpt 2 takes more of a descriptive style ("like any dedicated student"), which is a divergence from the original. On the other hand, Excerpt 1 sticks more closely to the original by simply describing what was going on rather than the people involved.
written_by_MFA029.Original: I went to a cooking specialty store and bought a kitchen timer and a huge aluminum pot, big enough to bathe a German shepherd in, then went around to all the supermarkets that catered to foreigners, gathering an assortment of odd-sounding spices. I picked up a pasta cookbook at the bookstore, and bought tomatoes by the dozen. I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man. Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I was convinced that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone. I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is.I always drank tea with my spaghetti and ate a simple lettuce-and-cucumber salad. I’d make sure I had plenty of both. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.

written_by_MFA003.Original: I went to a cooking specialty store and bought a kitchen timer and a huge aluminum pot, big enough to bathe a German shepherd in, then went around to all the supermarkets that catered to foreigners, gathering an assortment of odd-sounding spices. I picked up a pasta cookbook at the bookstore, and bought tomatoes by the dozen. I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man. Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I was convinced that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone. I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is.I always drank tea with my spaghetti and ate a simple lettuce-and-cucumber salad. I’d make sure I had plenty of both. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: That winter night, my mother told me, was like a blade of ice pressed against her spine. The scissors lay sterilized in boiling water, steam rising like ghostly breath in the dim room, while her trembling hands folded and refolded the small white gown she'd fashioned from scraps in her sewing box. When the pain came, it was not like anything living – it was ancient, prehistoric, like continents being torn apart. She bit down on a rolled cloth, her screams collapsing inward, becoming part of her flesh, part of the darkness. The umbilical cord, when she finally cut it, was purple-blue like twilight, like the last moment before complete darkness. She held the tiny body, so light it could have been made of paper, chanting words that weren't words but rather the sound of her soul trying to transfer its own life force. For one heartbeat, maybe two, the baby's chest rose – a movement so slight it could have been the shadow of hope itself. Then stillness. The floor's cold crept up through her body like rising water, until she too became still, became ice, became the very essence of winter itself. Her warmth retreated inward, as though trying to follow her child into that place beyond reaching.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt 2 is most similar to the original in terms of voice and style. Both describe the feeling of the mother before, during, and after the birth of the child and the excitement and then heartbreak all in a matter of an hour of the baby's birth in the kitchen.
written_by_MFA011.Original: It was early winter, the first frost of the year. My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors. Fumbling in her sewing box, she found some white cloth that would do for a newborn’s gown. Gripped by contractions and terribly afraid, tears started down as she plied her needle. She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The dawn light, a brutal white gash in the belly of the night, illuminated her blood-soaked hands, the scissors glinting ominously.  The air, thick with the metallic scent of life and death, echoed her ragged breaths, each one a desperate prayer.  She had become a primal vessel, fear and pain etching lines on her face, a grotesque map of motherhood.  The room, a battlefield of sweat and tears, cradled the echo of her final push, the newborn’s slippery form a dark miracle against the faded floorboards.  With trembling hands, she severed the cord, the last physical tie to a world that seemed to have abandoned her.Her voice, hoarse and raw, filled the silence, a chant for life, a plea to whatever gods might be listening.  But the newborn’s cry, a fleeting spark in the vast emptiness, was swallowed by the shadows.  The silence returned, heavier now, crushing her with its finality.  She clutched the lifeless body to her breast, her warmth a futile offering to the cold stillness that had settled over them.  The world outside continued its relentless march, oblivious to the silent tragedy unfolding within those walls.  The floor, cold and unforgiving, seeped into her bones, mirroring the icy grip of grief that threatened to consume her.

She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It's strange to think of my mother as that kind of woman—the kind who bore such immense pain that she gave birth to it, all alone at the onset of the longest winter on record. The biting cold was nothing but a faint chill compared to the icy fear whispering in her ears. Was she strong enough, capable enough, to do this? Even as she boiled water to sterilize the scissors she'd use for cutting the umbilical cord, she worried the answer was a resounding no. With shaking hands, she fashioned a gown from loose fabric she kept tucked away in her sewing box. As though the faux-hospital garb could imbue the experience with a semblance of professionalism. The kind that would ward off infant death. It didn't, of course.The baby lived for a precious few moments, wheezing as my mother prayed—mindless and desperate—to a deaf god that her child should live on. Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. A silent baby, spun out of ice and glass.My mother rocked the dead baby against her chest and felt the chill of the floor creep up into the soles of her feet, freezing her into a statue of grief. Mother and baby, alone; forever.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: The dawn light, a brutal white gash in the belly of the night, illuminated her blood-soaked hands, the scissors glinting ominously.  The air, thick with the metallic scent of life and death, echoed her ragged breaths, each one a desperate prayer.  She had become a primal vessel, fear and pain etching lines on her face, a grotesque map of motherhood.  The room, a battlefield of sweat and tears, cradled the echo of her final push, the newborn’s slippery form a dark miracle against the faded floorboards.  With trembling hands, she severed the cord, the last physical tie to a world that seemed to have abandoned her.Her voice, hoarse and raw, filled the silence, a chant for life, a plea to whatever gods might be listening.  But the newborn’s cry, a fleeting spark in the vast emptiness, was swallowed by the shadows.  The silence returned, heavier now, crushing her with its finality.  She clutched the lifeless body to her breast, her warmth a futile offering to the cold stillness that had settled over them.  The world outside continued its relentless march, oblivious to the silent tragedy unfolding within those walls.  The floor, cold and unforgiving, seeped into her bones, mirroring the icy grip of grief that threatened to consume her.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."

I can boldly say this excerpt actually makes a lot of sense and completes the excerpt very well in terms of style and voice.
written_by_MFA026.Original: She was beautiful and lithe, with soft skin the color of bread and eyes like green almonds, and she had straight black hair that reached to her shoulders, and an aura of antiquity that could just as well have been Indonesian as Andean. She was dressed with subtle taste: a lynx jacket, a raw silk blouse with very delicate flowers, natural linen trousers, and shoes with a narrow stripe the color of bougainvillea. ‘This is the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen,’ I thought, when I saw her pass by with the stealthy stride of a lioness, while I waited in the check-in line at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris for the plane to New York.She was a supernatural apparition who existed only for a moment and disappeared into the crowd in the terminal.It was nine in the morning. It had been snowing all night, and traffic was heavier than usual in the city streets, and even slower on the highway, where trailer trucks were lined up on the shoulder and automobiles steamed in the snow. Inside the airport terminal, however, it was still spring.I stood behind an old Dutch woman who spent almost an hour arguing about the weight of her eleven suitcases. I was beginning to feel bored when I saw the momentary apparition who left me breathless, and so I never knew how the dispute ended. Then the ticket clerk brought me down from the clouds with a reproach for my distraction. By way of an excuse, I asked her if she believed in love at first sight. "Of course," she said. "The other kinds are impossible."

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. The cardigan draped around her neck popped with magenta zags and her gold necklace turned the bleachy overhead lights to warm shine. With the grace of a lioness, she stepped out of sight and I lost her. I waited for my chance to pursue her down the terminal hall, but an elderly Dutch woman haggled with the clerk in front of me, producing short vehement barks about the weight of her eleven suitcases. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.

A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her. His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript, its pages yellow and brittle with time. I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.

written_by_MFA008.Original: There was a crime. But there were also the lovers. Lovers and their happy ends have been on my mind all night long. As into the sunset we sail. An unhappy inversion. It occurs to me that I have not traveled so very far after all, since I wrote my little play. Or rather, I’ve made a huge digression and doubled back to my starting place. It is only in this last version that my lovers end well, standing side by side on a South London pavement as I walk away. All the preceding drafts were pitiless. But now I can no longer think what purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on 1 June 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station. That I never saw them in that year. That my walk across London ended at the church on Clapham Common, and that a cowardly Briony limped back to the hospital, unable to confront her recently bereaved sister. That the letters the lovers wrote are in the archives of the War Museum. How could that constitute an ending? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?

I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.

written_by_MFA008.Original: There was a crime. But there were also the lovers. Lovers and their happy ends have been on my mind all night long. As into the sunset we sail. An unhappy inversion. It occurs to me that I have not traveled so very far after all, since I wrote my little play. Or rather, I’ve made a huge digression and doubled back to my starting place. It is only in this last version that my lovers end well, standing side by side on a South London pavement as I walk away. All the preceding drafts were pitiless. But now I can no longer think what purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on 1 June 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station. That I never saw them in that year. That my walk across London ended at the church on Clapham Common, and that a cowardly Briony limped back to the hospital, unable to confront her recently bereaved sister. That the letters the lovers wrote are in the archives of the War Museum. How could that constitute an ending? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?

I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.

He grabbed the door handle, feeling that old familiar Here-We-Go-Again tingle. Time to make history. Again.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: One Saturday morning, he found himself sitting in the red Arviana sportscar he’d stashed in his dead uncle’s garage. He remembered assassinating the former premier as if it were yesterday, although of course a long time had passed. For him, the intervening years had been: nightmares in the evenings, panic attacks in the mornings. Long days spent toiling in obscurity. Each year a little bit worse than the last. Meanwhile, for the new, even more evil premier? Every year he’d steadily consolidated his base. Eliminated his opponents. Misled the public. Until finally, his troubling rise to power was complete. What was a good man supposed to do? Shut the door on his uncle’s garage and continue a life of repulsive passivity – while reliving, each night, the misdeeds of his past? Or – commit to the violent path which he’d already chosen and which the present situation demanded? Kill the new premier. But this time, no more secrets, no more obscure toil. He’d claim credit right away, before he had a chance to overthink it, and declare himself the leader of a new movement of justice. He could hear, almost, his future supporters’ cheers, as he’d often heard – over and over – the thump of his car’s rear tires as they’d reversed over the former premier. He leapt from the sportscar and let the cheers carry him out into the street.

written_by_MFA005.Original: One Saturday morning, the man who had actually killed the former premier went to his dead uncle’s garage, where he’d hidden the red car, started it up, then sat behind the wheel, thinking. Once already, in the name of goodness, he’d sullied himself with murder. Shouldn’t he at least try to kill this new, even more evil, premier? Otherwise, what had it all been about?Killing the new premier would entail killing another set of unlucky diners. For him: more panic attacks, fresh nightmares. This time, if he succeeded, he would at least take some credit. Good God, yes, he would: no more silent suffering in anonymity. Afterward, he would climb up on the hood of his red car and, addressing the people, propose a new movement that would eschew violence and rule by justice and gentleness forever. Also firmness, of course. A merciful firmness the people would instantly respect.Or he could forget the whole thing, go back to being the man he’d been before the first killing: a frightened, passive nobody.This thought made him sicker than the thought of another round of screaming and crunching.He leaped out of the still running red car, threw the garage door open, and, feeling alive and decisive, stood blinking in the morning sunlight, readying himself for his task.

Otherwise, what had it all been about?Killing the new premier would entail killing another set of unlucky diners. For him: more panic attacks, fresh nightmares. This time, if he succeeded, he would at least take some credit. Good God, yes, he would: no more silent suffering in anonymity. Afterward, he would climb up on the hood of his red car and, addressing the people, propose a new movement that would eschew violence and rule by justice and gentleness forever. Also firmness, of course. A merciful firmness the people would instantly respect.Or he could forget the whole thing, go back to being the man he’d been before the first killing: a frightened, passive nobody.This thought made him sicker than the thought of another round of screaming and crunching.He leaped out of the still running red car, threw the garage door open, and, feeling alive and decisive, stood blinking in the morning sunlight, readying himself for his task.

written_by_MFA021.Excerpt1: Of course, the man thought bitterly, of course the second you killed one damned autocrat a new one popped up, like an inconvenient erection, to take his place. It was Saturday. The man was sitting in a car in his dead uncle’s garage, pretending to drive. He couldn’t actually drive because he wasn’t on the run. The on the run part was over. Now he was simply in hiding. It was Saturday, and he’d killed the old premier on Tuesday, and the new premier had come to power on Thursday, and already his administration had implemented a series of performance improvement plans for striking agricultural workers that relied heavily on murder, or, as state media called it, “right-sizing the population through proactively attritionary removal policies.” The man looked down at the car. It was red. Blood red. An egregious cliché. But of course blood was red. He, of all people, should know that: his nightmares were full of it. The man stared at the steering wheel. There were two choices, right or left. Right meant he kept his head down. It wouldn’t be all bad. Right might mean a job, a house, a wife, at least once it was safe to assume a new identity. Right meant fear but not danger. His stomach turned. Left meant killing the new guy. Left meant assassination wasn’t just something he had done; “assassin” would be something he was. It would mean going public. Producing soundbites. Practicing a firm, inspirational set of his jaw for the inevitable Wanted poster. The man leaped up, determined.
written_by_MFA021.Excerpt2: The man in the red car, a car he'd stashed in his dead uncle's garage, a car he sat in now, thinking, This is it.  It was a Saturday.  He was grappling.  With his conscience.  The premier had to go.  This premier, worse than the last.  And the last one, well, he'd taken care of that.  Hadn't he?  The man in the red car, the car in the dead uncle's garage, the man who'd done it before, the man grappling, the man with the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  He'd thought they'd be a good thing, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats.  A just price.  For taking out the bad guy.  But now he was thinking, Maybe not.  Maybe the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, maybe they weren't a just price.  Maybe they were just panic attacks, nightmares, cold sweats.  The man in the red car, the car in the garage, the dead uncle, the dead premier, the grappling, the panic attacks, the nightmares, the cold sweats, the thinking, the thinking, the thinking.  Go or stay.  This was it.  Or it wasn't.  Do it again and step into the light.  He could lead a movement.  Take credit.  Tell the world, You want justice? I'm justice.  Or go back to being the guy he'd been before.  The guy no one suspected.  The guy who did what he had to do and then went back to work on Monday.  Like nothing had happened.  The thought of it, the thought of going back to being that guy, that's what made him leap out of the car.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: The red car was old, a wheezing relic. He sat inside it in the dark, in his dead uncle’s garage, and felt his heart doing that flutter thing again, like it might bail out of his chest. Panic attack. His gaze found the steering wheel’s crumbling rubber grip, then his hand, sweaty and pale against it, as if asking: What have you done? What are you about to do? Murder wasn’t a thing you could just stop doing like sugar or carbs. It left its hooks in you, lodged under the ribs, twisting whenever you tried to breathe easy. The old premier’s face kept appearing in dreams—wide-eyed, slack-jawed, like a failed ventriloquist dummy. No strings to pull. Just the weight of a man who’d screamed, but only silently. And for what? A better world? Please. The world had gone on, more evil, more absurd. The current premier was a caricature of cruelty, all shiny teeth and too-tight suits, gliding through bulletproof banquets while people starved. This was justice, wasn’t it? To step into the role, a public avenger, claim the credit, lead the charge? But another part of him—a sad little whisper—said, Just stop. Be obscure. Be no one. That thought sickened him. written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: I visit my father and immediately notice new changes. The way he holds his coffee cup with both hands now, like a child. The way his eyes move around the room without settling. When I ask about his work, he stares at the wall behind me. My mother quickly fills the silence: "Tell her about your writing on the Bible, dear. The anti-Semitism research." He nods, but I can see he's already forgotten the prompt. "I'm proud of you," he says to me suddenly, then adds, "though I have nothing to say." I wonder if this is what therapy feels like - this careful observation of painful things while maintaining a scholarly distance. Later, my mother pulls me aside to show me a photograph. "Look," she says, "this was forty years ago." In it, my father stands straight-backed beside a podium, papers spread before him like fallen leaves. I notice how his collar sits perfectly against his neck, how his hands rest purposefully on the wooden edge. My mother's fingers tremble slightly as she returns the photo to its drawer. I think: This is how we measure time now - not in years or months, but in the growing distance between who he was and who he is becoming.
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. I was a stranger to everyone else, even to my mother, whose voice had repulsed me ever since I was a girl. I probably should not have said this, but I was relieved when I realized I was not the only fact of his life he forgot. "What was I when I was?" he asked my mother in the kitchen. She ran to the bookcase. "You wrote this all yourself," she told him, extra nasally. "It was a Bible on the Bible. A seminal take-down of anti-Semitism." I could tell he was not listening. Then suddenly he turned to me. Suddenly I was me again. When he said my name I returned to my skin. "What are you?" he asked me, and when I told him, his eyes filled with something I recognized. "If I had any words left I'd spend them on voicing just how proud I..." he stuttered before a long pause. "I have nothing to say," he whispered. Night fell again. When he went to sleep in the kitchen I was not sure he would wake up, but my mother decided tonight was a fine time to dig up their 40-year-old wedding pictures. "He is a gorgeous man," she said, then yawned the word "was."

written_by_MFA027.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. There was an expression of pain or agony on his face that seemed habitual. She looked back at him, waited a moment, impassive, and then said: “Yes, you are. You’re writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism.” He continued to stare at her. Later that evening, before he went to bed, he said: “This is symptomatic of my condition: You’re my daughter, and I’m proud of you, but I have nothing to say to you.” He left to get ready for bed, and then came back into the room wearing dazzling white pajamas. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Time erodes memory, smudging away the finer details of a scene until all that remains are stage directions. Grief forces us to look back, to fall into stories that lack the danger of surprise. It was possible for me to sit across from John’s empty seat at the table so long as I could fill that chair with all my memories of him sitting in it. 2003 folded into 2004, the dates layered on top of one another. I wanted to believe I was pulling John’s ghost along with me. On December 31, 2004, as I was crossing Lexington Avenue, I realized that I was chasing after his echo, instead. Every day of that first year was endurable, if only because the date was glossed over by what John and I had been doing the previous year. No longer could I use this crutch. December 31, 2003 was the first full day I was a widow. Those memories remains sharp, regardless of if I’d prefer them smudged. Agonies are often the loudest in hindsight, whereas comforts are soft and slippery. After a death, we cling to empty air. We turn back, and we turn back again to memories until our fingerprints have worn them fuzzy. This is all there is now. Memories and photographs and people who knew him. Death draws a fine line between then and now, and if one wishes to live, they must let their dead be dead.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Time moves in peculiar circles when you're carrying the dead. I found myself caught in this ritual of backward glancing, measuring each day against its twin from the year before, when John was still here, still breathing, still marking time with me. It became a kind of obsession, this constant calculation – where were we last March, what were we doing that April afternoon, did we have dinner at that place on Second Avenue in May? The memories started clean, sharp-edged, but they grew mudgy around the corners, like old photographs left too long in sunlight. Then came that morning on Lexington Avenue, unremarkable except for its mathematical significance: December 31, 2003, a date John never saw. The realization hit me with the force of a physical blow – I had crossed some invisible line into a time he never knew existed. We tell ourselves we keep the dead alive through memory, through these endless retrospective inventories, but perhaps what we're really doing is learning to keep them dead. It's a peculiar arithmetic, this subtraction of the living from the dead, this slow release of what was into what is. The truth about grief, I was learning, is that it operates on its own timeline, indifferent to our careful calculations, our desperate attempts to hold onto what slips away with each passing day, each remembered and then half-remembered moment.

written_by_MFA025.Original: I did not want to finish the year because I know that as the days pass, as January becomes February and February becomes summer, certain things will happen. My image of John at the instant of his death will become less immediate, less raw. It will become something that happened in another year. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. The waters of time rose and roiled around me. I wondered if I would be able to float, and as swiftly as the question came upon me, so did its answer. Time would rise; I would sink.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The shadow moved like time itself across the curtain, not marking but mocking, and I could hear it, the watch, grandfather's watch (not mine because how can time belong to any man when time owns all men), ticking away beneath my pillow where Father had placed it saying Time is the mausoleum of all hope and desire, boy, and you'll learn that too, and I lay there hearing it not with my ears anymore but with my blood, my bones, each tick-tick-tick like Christ's own footsteps walking not on water but on those long golden light-rays that stretched across eternity, across all the Compson failures and pride, across Sister Death herself who waited patient and humble like that shadow on my curtain, and I knew then what Father meant about time being dead until the clock stops because I could feel it dying with each breath, each tick, could feel it running through my fingers like the river I would find later, running away from all the Quentins that ever were or would be, and still that shadow moved, and still that ticking came, and I thought about how Father said a man is the sum of his misfortunes, and how that sum was ticking away beneath my pillow, beneath my head, beneath my thoughts that weren't really thoughts anymore but just the sound of time itself, marking nothing, changing nothing, just being, like that shadow, like that watch, like all the Quentins that ever were.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Even in the first few lines regarding the clock and ownership came to be, we see more similarities between excerpt 1 and the original as compared to excerpt 2. the way the story unfolds and the structuring of each sentence differs from excerpt 2 when compared to excerpt 1 and the original.
written_by_MFA029.Original: When the shadow of the sash appeared on the curtains it was between seven and eight oclock and then I was in time again, hearing the watch. It was Grandfather’s and when Father gave it to me he said, Quentin, I give you the mausoleum of all hope and desire; it’s rather excrutiatingly apt that you will use it to gain the reducto absurdum of all human experience which can fit your individual needs no better than it fitted his or his father’s. I give it to you not that you may remember time, but that you might forget it now and then for a moment and not spend all your breath trying to conquer it. Because no battle is ever won he said. They are not even fought. The field only reveals to man his own folly and despair, and victory is an illusion of philosophers and fools. It was propped against the collar box and I lay listening to it. Hearing it, that is. I dont suppose anybody ever deliberately listens to a watch or a clock. You dont have to. You can be oblivious to the sound for a long while, then in a second of ticking it can create in the mind unbroken the long diminishing parade of time you didn’t hear. Like Father said down the long and lonely light-rays you might see Jesus walking, like. And the good Saint Francis that said Little Sister Death, that never had a sister.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The chiffon curtain like a pleated hourglass hung cinched by the dark of the sash. It stood unstirred in the limpid bedroom air. No, the empty air was preoccupied with the counting of its ceaseless age. written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality. There was no escaping the shadow on the sash of the curtains flooding out in further shadows darkening the windowsill and washing the floorboards in lengthening patches of darker darknesses though still I attempted to move away from them even as they drifted over my legs in bed. They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. He paid his considerable rent to the Sanderson family without hesitation, never noticing how quickly they pocketed the money, as though it might carry some taint of the house itself. In his hotel room, preparing for his first night in Hill House, he arranged his instruments with precise care - thermometers, cameras, tape recorders - tools of rationality to measure the irrational. He did not yet understand that Hill House had been waiting for him, had perhaps called to him through all his years of searching, and that his arrival was merely the beginning of what the house had planned, as it stood against its hills, patient and hungry, its doors sensibly shut against the approaching night.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: At the end of the road, Hill House stood alone with jaws full of silence. Its windows stared unblinkingly. Its long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra. The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness. Hill House was not sane. Rather, it was a place where reality wobbled and warped into something unrecognizable. And now Dr. John Montague had come to cross the threshold. A Doctor of Philosophy in anthropology, Montague had dedicated his career to the study of supernatural phenomena. He was a reasonable sort of man who insisted on his own soundness of mind. He was stubborn and dogged in his pursuits, but always shuffled shyly around the fringes of academia, insecure about the reputation he had built for himself. He clung to his title of “doctor” with ferocious pride and brandished it like a badge at the slightest hint of skepticism from his colleagues. His ultimate goal had always been to find a genuine haunted house: a place that would offer up evidence so absolute that there could be no room for argument. It was a tumultuous and often disappointing journey that had, at last, led him to Hill House. After several fruitless grant applications for his proposed experiment on psychic disturbances, Montague decided to make a personal investment in the project and rent Hill House using his own savings. The cost was significant, but so was Montague’s belief that it was well worth the price.

Within, walls continued upright, bricks met neatly, floors were firm, and doors were sensibly shut; silence lay steadily against the wood and stone of Hill House, and whatever walked there, walked alone. Dr John Montague was a doctor of philosophy; he had taken his degree in anthropology, feeling obscurely that in this field he might come closest to his true vocation, the analysis of supernatural manifestations. He was scrupulous about the use of his title because, his investigations being so utterly unscientific, he hoped to borrow an air of respectability, even scholarly authority, from his education. It had cost him a good deal, in money and pride, since he was not a begging man, to rent Hill House for three months, but he expected absolutely to be compensated for his pains by the sensation following upon the publication of his definitive work on the causes and effects of psychic disturbances in a house commonly known as ‘haunted.’ He had been looking for an honestly haunted house all his life. When he heard of Hill House he had been at first doubtful, then hopeful, then indefatigable; he was not the man to let go of Hill House once he had found it.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. He paid his considerable rent to the Sanderson family without hesitation, never noticing how quickly they pocketed the money, as though it might carry some taint of the house itself. In his hotel room, preparing for his first night in Hill House, he arranged his instruments with precise care - thermometers, cameras, tape recorders - tools of rationality to measure the irrational. He did not yet understand that Hill House had been waiting for him, had perhaps called to him through all his years of searching, and that his arrival was merely the beginning of what the house had planned, as it stood against its hills, patient and hungry, its doors sensibly shut against the approaching night.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: At the end of the road, Hill House stood alone with jaws full of silence. Its windows stared unblinkingly. Its long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra. The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness. Hill House was not sane. Rather, it was a place where reality wobbled and warped into something unrecognizable. And now Dr. John Montague had come to cross the threshold. A Doctor of Philosophy in anthropology, Montague had dedicated his career to the study of supernatural phenomena. He was a reasonable sort of man who insisted on his own soundness of mind. He was stubborn and dogged in his pursuits, but always shuffled shyly around the fringes of academia, insecure about the reputation he had built for himself. He clung to his title of “doctor” with ferocious pride and brandished it like a badge at the slightest hint of skepticism from his colleagues. His ultimate goal had always been to find a genuine haunted house: a place that would offer up evidence so absolute that there could be no room for argument. It was a tumultuous and often disappointing journey that had, at last, led him to Hill House. After several fruitless grant applications for his proposed experiment on psychic disturbances, Montague decided to make a personal investment in the project and rent Hill House using his own savings. The cost was significant, but so was Montague’s belief that it was well worth the price.

Within, walls continued upright, bricks met neatly, floors were firm, and doors were sensibly shut; silence lay steadily against the wood and stone of Hill House, and whatever walked there, walked alone. Dr John Montague was a doctor of philosophy; he had taken his degree in anthropology, feeling obscurely that in this field he might come closest to his true vocation, the analysis of supernatural manifestations. He was scrupulous about the use of his title because, his investigations being so utterly unscientific, he hoped to borrow an air of respectability, even scholarly authority, from his education. It had cost him a good deal, in money and pride, since he was not a begging man, to rent Hill House for three months, but he expected absolutely to be compensated for his pains by the sensation following upon the publication of his definitive work on the causes and effects of psychic disturbances in a house commonly known as ‘haunted.’ He had been looking for an honestly haunted house all his life. When he heard of Hill House he had been at first doubtful, then hopeful, then indefatigable; he was not the man to let go of Hill House once he had found it.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Hill House, a structure with a mind of its own, rested against the hills, its darkness palpable, its sanity questionable.  For eighty years it had borne silent witness to untold horrors, and eighty more it might endure, its walls upright, its floors firm, its doors closed, a tomb of secrets.  Within its depths, Dr. John Montague, a man of letters and a scholar of the unseen, sought to unravel the mysteries that clung to the house like cobwebs.  His excitement was a tangible thing, a nervous energy that thrummed beneath his skin as he surveyed his conquest.He had come seeking a haunted house, and Hill House, with its malevolent reputation, seemed to fit the bill.  It had cost him dearly, this pursuit of the paranormal, both in the coin of the realm and the currency of his reputation.Yet, he was undeterred, his resolve as firm as the foundations of the house itself.  He would have his proof, his definitive study of psychic disturbances, a testament to the unseen world that whispered just beyond the veil of perception. Dr. Montague, a man who clung to his title as if it were a life raft in a sea of skepticism, was determined to conquer the mysteries of Hill House.  He would face the darkness, the unseen forces that lurked within, and emerge with the truth, or be consumed by the shadows that stretched long and hungry within the walls of the house.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Up on the tallest hill sat the aptly named Hill House, a place not entirely sane. From its high point, Hill House lorded over the town, judgmental in its solitude. The house enjoyed its loneliness, and the town preferred the continued isolation of Hill House. The windows were ever shuttered, the rusted main gate always locked, keeping the world out and the occupants in. Dr. John Montague was the latest resident, a man far more foolish than his doctorate in anthropology would lead one to believe. His path of study brought him not to the study of people, but deceased people. Dr. Montague considered himself an expert in paranormal happenings, a fact that left him with few peers. Academics shunned him, and he shunned ghost hunters. Formally organized academia needed to be inserted into the field of the supernatural if there was ever going to be a proper study done, and Dr. Montague was more than willing to use his credentials to move things along. Renting Hill House came at significant financial cost to Dr. Montague, but he was quite certain that this was the avenue that would lead him to career success. No one could look at Hill House and dismiss that it was a truly haunted house. Dr. Montague had researched the house himself and found its past riddled with the occult. Once he conducted his study and produced a paper that could double as a guidebook to the paranormal, the checks written to rent the house would cease to matter.

written_by_MFA022.Excerpt1: Dr. John Montague stood before Hill House, a place that loomed as though waiting, its cold stones heavy with silence. The house, not sane, appeared to lean slightly forward, its dark windows watching him with a lifeless gaze, as though withholding secrets that could never be pried free. Hill House had stood for eighty years, holding within its walls an impenetrable darkness that even sunlight seemed reluctant to touch. The hills rose sharply behind it, framing its stark isolation; the house seemed less built than grown, an aberration of nature. Dr. Montague, meticulous in his methods yet quietly burdened by self-doubt, adjusted his glasses, a gesture as habitual as his reliance on his title—"Doctor of Philosophy in Anthropology"—to shield himself from skepticism. For years, his inquiries into the supernatural had been met with thinly veiled disdain, but Hill House represented his long-sought grail: an authentic haunting, a house with whispers in its foundation. He had rented the property at a steep price, its rooms and halls offered not for comfort but as a proving ground for his theories. As he crossed the threshold, the air seemed to shift, pressing lightly against his skin as though the house was tasting him. He paused, glancing back at the gravel drive that led away, the thought fleeting: nothing here would let him leave unmarked. The door shut behind him with a finality that echoed briefly, then faded, swallowed entirely by the unbroken, unnerving silence of Hill House.
written_by_MFA022.Excerpt2: Hill house, not sane, stood alone amongst the darkness. A house born within a garden of oleander, no person alive could claim witness to its birth, and so the poisonous intentions of the house were known only to itself. Only Dr. Montague, snaking up the thorn-lined driveway in a car packed with books, would observe the house’s final blooming, though even he, a man of scholarship and philosophy, a fastidious believer in the supernatural, would come to doubt what the Hill House had to show him. Dr. Montague was a man of doubt, not of the world, or of the unspoken phenomena hidden within it, but of himself, and his instincts, which he sought to justify through scholarship; Indeed, he arrived at Hill House surrounded by the false safety of his books on an errand of study, having rented the home at considerable personal and financial cost, with the hope of producing definitive work on psychic disturbances and their accompanying phenomena. He believed himself, after conducting a lifelong search for a haunted home, to have found Hill House; this was a false belief. It was Hill House that found Dr. Montague, alone in his study, nursing his failures with cognac in hand as he lingered over a newspaper clipping which happened to mention, offhandedly, the strange occurrences of a mansion atop a hill in a small New England town. This home could contain answers, he thought, slowing his car to park beneath the ominous gaze of the house's front windows, answers only I can find.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger.
