written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. Her voice was steady but her hands shook as she arranged and rearranged the little heap of mail on her bedside table. I thought about my own mail piling up at home—how long would I need to stay?—and felt ashamed for thinking of such things. The practical always intrudes on the sacred, I suppose. She spoke of her body's betrayals with a kind of weary impatience, the way you might discuss a chronically late friend who nevertheless remained dear to you. Don't ask me about the pills, she said. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.

written_by_MFA029.Original: We could have it for a month, she told me over the phone. Not that I think I’ll need that much time.Would I ever get used to this kind of talk? Even as I wondered what to do about my mail—let it pile up, have the post office forward it or hold it for me—I found it unthinkable to ask how long I should plan to be gone.It’s not like I’ve picked a date, she said. Though, as I say, I am ready to go. You could even say I’m impatient to go, which comes partly from my having already given so much thought to dying but also from having reached the limits of what I think I can bear. But I don’t know what my body will do.Though she’d been feeling much better since she went off chemo, her symptoms could change from day to day, and the meds she was taking to suppress them had some side effects too.In any case, I want things to happen naturally, she said. I feel like I’ll know when it’s time.But you—well, you won’t know, she said. Obviously I won’t be making a big announcement. Like the coming of the Lord, she said jokingly: You will not know the day or hour.She had decided not to tell anyone about our plans. I’ve come this far, I don’t want to risk some stupid intervention, she said, or even a tiny disruption. I want peace.No one was to know where we were.And, for your own protection, she told me, you need to play dumb: I never told you what I was going to do, you weren’t even aware that I had the drug.I had, in fact, already told one other person everything, but I did not say this.

written_by_MFA029.Original: We could have it for a month, she told me over the phone. Not that I think I’ll need that much time.Would I ever get used to this kind of talk? Even as I wondered what to do about my mail—let it pile up, have the post office forward it or hold it for me—I found it unthinkable to ask how long I should plan to be gone.It’s not like I’ve picked a date, she said. Though, as I say, I am ready to go. You could even say I’m impatient to go, which comes partly from my having already given so much thought to dying but also from having reached the limits of what I think I can bear. But I don’t know what my body will do.Though she’d been feeling much better since she went off chemo, her symptoms could change from day to day, and the meds she was taking to suppress them had some side effects too.In any case, I want things to happen naturally, she said. I feel like I’ll know when it’s time.But you—well, you won’t know, she said. Obviously I won’t be making a big announcement. Like the coming of the Lord, she said jokingly: You will not know the day or hour.She had decided not to tell anyone about our plans. I’ve come this far, I don’t want to risk some stupid intervention, she said, or even a tiny disruption. I want peace.No one was to know where we were.And, for your own protection, she told me, you need to play dumb: I never told you what I was going to do, you weren’t even aware that I had the drug.I had, in fact, already told one other person everything, but I did not say this.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. Her voice was steady but her hands shook as she arranged and rearranged the little heap of mail on her bedside table. I thought about my own mail piling up at home—how long would I need to stay?—and felt ashamed for thinking of such things. The practical always intrudes on the sacred, I suppose. She spoke of her body's betrayals with a kind of weary impatience, the way you might discuss a chronically late friend who nevertheless remained dear to you. Don't ask me about the pills, she said. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I made him promise not to tell.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: She’d said, “I want to handle this in my own way, on my own terms.”Her words hung in the air, heavy with finality and a hint of defiance.“I’m tired of waiting,” she continued, her voice a mix of weariness and determination.“I’m tired of this body failing me, of the endless treatments, the uncertainty.”She spoke of wanting to die peacefully, naturally, without any interference.“I don’t want any interventions, any disruptions,” she’d said.“I don’t want anyone trying to prolong this… existence.” She paused, a wry smile flickering across her face.“I don’t want anyone trying to play God,” she added, her tone a blend of humor and solemnity.Her words echoed in my mind as I walked down the street, the weight of our conversation pressing on me.I thought about her situation, her desire for autonomy, her frustration with the slow, unpredictable decay of her body.I thought about her wish for a peaceful, natural death, her refusal to let anyone “play God.”I thought about her insistence on secrecy, her plea for me not to mention her plans to anyone, not even my closest confidantes.I felt a knot of tension tighten in my chest, a conflict between my loyalty to her and my own need to process this heavy situation.I thought about the consequences of her choice, the potential legal ramifications, the emotional toll it would take on those who cared about her. I thought about my own role in this, my promise to support her, my fear of being implicated, my desire to protect her and myself.I felt a surge of guilt, a sense of betrayal, as I remembered the conversation I’d had with my therapist, the one person I’d confided in, breaking my promise to her.I tried to justify my actions, telling myself that I needed someone to talk to, someone to help me navigate this emotional minefield.But the guilt lingered, a constant reminder of my broken promise.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Jack stood there, fists balled in his jacket pockets, words tearing out of him like barbed wire through flesh. "Twenty years we been at this, En. The moment passed like so many before it, settling into the collection of hurts they carried, weight added to weight until the burden seemed natural as breathing.

written_by_MFA015.Reason:
The reason why it works is that it is raw and unfiltered, as though something that has been held in over the years and then finally exploded. Jack's speech is disordered, monotonous, and furious, but that is precisely what makes it closer to reality. He is also in a repetitive cycle of the same pain they experience when they are desperate and exhausted. The phrases such as Count the damn few times we've been together in twenty years and, I wish I knew how to quit you are not musical in their sound, they sound forced, and they sound screeched out, and that sincerity is what makes the scene.
The surroundings of Ennis are no less effective in the narration. His breakdown comes rather fast and almost clumsily, and is not preceded by any emotional climax, which makes it even more striking. The fact that things are snapping back nearly to the position they had been speaks volumes about their relationship more than any description would have. Nothing is established, nothing bursts out in transformation--and there is the tragedy.
The second passage interprets the feeling, but it describes too much. Instead of being left to shock, the breakdown of Ennis is spelled out, and Jack is more articulate than he should be in the moment. It smoothens the edges, and the edges are the point.

Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Kant writes the email and spends a long time editing it, making minor changes to the wording only to change them back to exactly what he’d written before. He thinks about his upbringing and all the years that this information has weighed on him: the kids in middle school who tackled him in the locker room and forced him to eat dog shit, the fact that he couldn’t even admit to himself that he wanted to watch gay porn until he was twenty-five. Paralyzed, still editing, he imagines his mother’s disgust upon reading the email, imagining her 31-year-old son doing exactly what he’d done for the better part of the last two decades: that is, fanatasizing about some buff, hairy dude he saw online. He imagines himself dying alone, ostracized from anyone who might love him, the nerves in his dick beginning to desensitize from too much dry-hand masturbation. When he sends the email, though, the responses are surprisingly anticlimactic. He gets a few heart emojis from friends; some coworkers reply with “nice,” and “good for you!” Even his parents are mostly supportive, though his mom expresses some mild annoyance that he hadn’t called first to warn them. Kant feels a mixture of intense relief, combined with an unpleasant sense of disappointment that he finds difficult to face. Where was the fallout, the dramatic messages and cut-off relationships from family members? Why didn’t anyone care? He had once imagined his post-coming out life as a time of transformation, a new life like a beautiful patterned carpet rolling out before him, but instead he finds himself stuck in the exact same state of stasis that emboldened him to write the email in the first place. He begins to call this period his “Year of Damp Feet,” as his feet are constantly sweaty despite the fact that he rarely moves them from beneath his computer desk.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Kant spent hours drafting the email, toggling between subject lines (“A Word to Everyone,” “FYI,” and, finally, “Coming Out”) like they were tarot cards predicting his fate. In his head, each recipient’s reaction unspooled in unrelenting technicolor: his mother, weeping silently in the kitchen as she diced onions for the biryani she thought would fix his mood; his old college roommate forwarding the email to their group chat with the caption, “Knew it”; his boss, furrowing his brow at the computer, typing, “Not sure why this concerns me professionally.” These imagined catastrophes paraded through his thoughts as he clicked send, his trembling hand a cheap metaphor for the fear wedged in his sternum. Then: nothing. The world didn’t combust. Instead, his notifications flooded with low-stakes affirmations—heart emojis from friends, a “proud of you, dude” text from a cousin, even a begrudging “love you” from his father, which Kant suspected had been typed under duress from his mother. He should’ve felt relief, triumph even, but instead, there was this sneaking, hollow ache. He’d braced himself for rejection, a narrative arc with stakes, but life handed him a shrug and a pat on the back. What was the point of all that dread if no one made it cinematic? The next few weeks stretched out like an overcooked spaghetti noodle—soft, limp, no bite. Without the anticipated martyrdom, Kant drifted into what he called his “Year of Damp Feet,” shuffling around his apartment in unwashed socks, ignoring texts inviting him to “finally celebrate.” He scrolled through his inbox, rereading replies, hoping to stumble on something more… dramatic. Wasn’t this supposed to be the pivot point of his life? Instead, he remained unchanged, realizing that even monumental self-revelations couldn’t save him from the everyday inertia of being Kant. A hero’s journey, sure—but with no villain, no fight, just the lukewarm end credits rolling over silence.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Mrs. Dalloway, stepping out into the June morning, thought how she would fetch the flowers herself, for Lucy had quite enough to manage with those men from Rumpelmayer's coming. It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.

written_by_MFA026.Original: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.For Lucy had her work cut out for her. The doors would be taken off their hinges; Rumpelmayer’s men were coming. And then, thought Clarissa Dalloway, what a morning — fresh as if issued to children on a beach.What a lark! What a plunge! He must have said it at breakfast one morning when she had gone out on to the terrace — Peter Walsh. He would be back from India one of these days, June or July, she forgot which, for his letters were awfully dull; it was his sayings one remembered; his eyes, his pocket-knife, his smile, his grumpiness and, when millions of things had utterly vanished — how strange it was! — a few sayings like this about cabbages.

Peter Walsh (he was coming back from India, his letters said) had laughed at her that morning at breakfast, saying she preferred men to cauliflowers — how like him to say such a thing, to pierce through to some truth while making it all seem ridiculous! His letters, scattered now across her desk at home like fallen leaves, still carried that sharp wit, that capacity to wound and heal in the same breath. And how strange it was, she thought, pausing at the corner of Bond Street, that while whole years dissolved into nothing, that single moment remained: Peter's fork suspended, his eyes twinkling with mischief, the morning light streaming across the breakfast table at Bourton. The way he would tilt his head when amused (she could see it now, with perfect clarity) while all else blurred and shifted like patterns in water. For that was what memory did, was it not? It preserved these fragments, these bright shards of experience, while whole seasons fell away into darkness, into that great pool of forgotten things that lay beneath the surface of one's daily life.

written_by_MFA026.Original: Mrs. Dalloway said she would buy the flowers herself.For Lucy had her work cut out for her. The doors would be taken off their hinges; Rumpelmayer’s men were coming. And then, thought Clarissa Dalloway, what a morning — fresh as if issued to children on a beach.What a lark! What a plunge! For so it had always seemed to her, when, with a little squeak of the hinges, which she could hear now, she had burst open the French windows and plunged at Bourton into the open air. How fresh, how calm, stiller than this of course, the air was in the early morning; like the flap of a wave; the kiss of a wave; chill and sharp and yet (for a girl of eighteen as she then was) solemn, feeling as she did, standing there at the open window, that something awful was about to happen; looking at the flowers, at the trees with the smoke winding off them and the rooks rising, falling; standing and looking until Peter Walsh said, “Musing among the vegetables?”— was that it? —“I prefer men to cauliflowers”— was that it? He must have said it at breakfast one morning when she had gone out on to the terrace — Peter Walsh. He would be back from India one of these days, June or July, she forgot which, for his letters were awfully dull; it was his sayings one remembered; his eyes, his pocket-knife, his smile, his grumpiness and, when millions of things had utterly vanished — how strange it was! — a few sayings like this about cabbages.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: She had decided to buy the flowers herself, to spare Lucy the trouble — Lucy, who was rushing about with preparations for the party, and Rumpelmayer’s men were about also; Yes, thought Mrs Dalloway, I will buy them myself. It was all coming together as many parties had done before, with great bustle, and would come together in the end as all parties do, as did those parties from her youth when she was not the host. And the fresh morning air returns her to younger days at Bourton, stepping out into other early mornings — how exhilarating it was then, and how solemn also, to be eighteen and just beginning. The chill this air carries, and the slow warmth rising into one’s cheeks, and ears, and hands. What had Peter said to me: something about cauliflowers, about preferring men to cauliflowers. A conversation over breakfast with Peter Walsh, always teasing then; still teasing now, albeit separated by so many years and kilometres. Clarissa thinks of his letters, the glint in his eye she can still feel in those pages — his promise, too, steady as his voice, to return from India, to return and to see her. Cauliflowers! Such a thing to remember as clearly as if their breakfast was shared only yesterday, when in fact yesterday Clarissa had been deciding about the flowers, deciding to buy them from the yellow and blue shop she now rapidly approaches, with the vibrant window displays; the freshest flowers, she knew, those with the richest and most enduring smell, must come from this shop, and now she would buy them herself.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The morning air reunited Clarissa Dalloway with Bourton, her younger face and younger days, her eighteen-year-old solemnity. She had a bright evening ahead, an ambition to entertain Rumplemayer's men. She was in wonder among the flowers, having traversed the market in lieu of her servant, Lucy. The young girl deserved a break, an evening to mind her own affairs. What else was a girl but this? But back to Bourton, where the air had kissed Clarissa's cheeks like the finest gentleman, where Peter Walsh had teased her over breakfast, asserting that cauliflowers were surely superior to men. He was on a sojourn in India, which he'd detailed in rambling letters. His letters were stiffened by truisms, cloyingly personal, a bore to spend one's evening with. What Clarissa recalled most were his teeth, their hue of yellow, not unhygienic but telling of inferior genetics. He had a laugh like a doctor's, inappropriate. He'd tell you about your muggy insides, then chuckle because there was nothing wrong with his. But alas, the flowers. Lavender or Rose? This called to mind Peter again and his oddly feminine smells. That he smelled unlike a man endeared Clarissa to him. Scent was a signature, a tell of how one moved through the world. To share a scent with a woman, one must also share her sensibilities, her gentleness, her sense of utter safety. If Peter were to return early, to meet Clarissa in the market right then, she'd recognize his teeth first, then his scent. She'd think how familiar the dull yellow of his mouth was. Admittedly, his remaining details might strike her as unfamiliar.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.

written_by_MFA012.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.

It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.

written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: The night air, maybe tinged with the scent of some flowering tree I can’t identify, swirls through the gaps in the fencing.  The thrill elicited by this view—the tiny illuminated windows, the way human-scale elements are visibly enmeshed with the inhuman scale of the skyline—is something I associate with urban spaces.  The Hudson River, the Palisades on the other side, even the movement of the clouds, fail to trigger the same response.I breathe deeply, trying to identify the chemical compounds in the air.  I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens.  I imagine the collective exhalation of eight million people, the collective inhalation, the movement of hands over innumerable screens, the scrolling, the tapping, the repetitive stress injuries.  I picture the vast network of pipes, mains, and cables extending below the streets, the nighttime deliveries to bodegas, the movement of trains underground.I see the skyline as the material manifestation of a second person plural, a collective to which all art, even the most intimate, is addressed.  A yet-to-exist “we” glimpsed in the bundled debt, the traces of antidepressants in the water supply, the elaborate traffic system, the weather patterns.  I resolve to become the kind of artist who can transform bad forms of collectivity—bedbugs, or the crowds now surging toward Times Square—into glimpses of their potential for a kind of unity, a communal body.    And then there’s Noor, around whom the fiction of the world reorganizes itself.  I’m always trying to get back to her, but she’s never fully available, and this unavailability is central to her function.  She’s here, but only in the form of a promise I’ve made to myself to get up early and run the loop of the park, a promise I’ve already broken.I’m trying to think my way into a future state, but I’m too aware of my body on the bench to achieve the desired self-alienation.  I feel the pressure of the chain-link fence against my back, the bandanna flattening my hair.  I’m eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice running down my chin.  I’m having a mild lacrimal event, quietly tearing up.I’m never fully identical with myself.  There’s always a part of me that’s alien to me.  And this is where the hope, the utopian glimmer, resides—in the self-estrangement that enables me to imagine the past and present merging into something reinterpreted, whole.

You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.

written_by_MFA008.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. The tears are neither despair nor ecstasy but a texture of the moment, the salt of an urban meditation that hovers between the profound and the ridiculous. I do not attempt to resolve it, knowing the real art is in letting the tension linger, illuminating the skyline from within.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.

I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I was a boy of World War II and a boy of Newark. The war was far away and beyond my understanding, but the dread and threat of it spilled across the ocean and flooded every home in my city. Lots of our men were off fighting, and lots of them would never come home. Rations of oil and sugar were dispensed through clenched fists. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Swede. It was a name that echoed through the streets of Weequahic like a myth in the making. Seymour Irving Levov, the golden-haired boy with eyes as blue as the summer sky, a figure so different from the rest of us, the dark-haired, sallow-skinned sons of Abraham. He was an anomaly, a beautiful paradox in our world of traditions and books, where the mind was king and the body a mere vessel. Yet, there he was, our very own Apollo, a god in cleats and a varsity jacket, conquering not with intellect but with the raw power of his physique.He was a football hero, a basketball star, a baseball legend, all rolled into one. He wasn't just playing these games; he was dominating them, bending them to his will with the same effortless grace that seemed to permeate his every move. And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. And in those dark days, when the future seemed so uncertain, we needed that dream, we needed that myth, we needed the Swede.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. What I remember most about that time is not the constant barrage of terrible news or the hushed conversations about the Germans, but rather a boy, well, a young man, named Seymour Irving Levov, though we all called him “The Swede,” because he looked about as Nordic as they come with his white-blond hair and his blue eyes, all the Jewishness rinsed out of him at birth. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. You would have seen a group of people utterly unafraid.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Newark, during those tense years of World War II, there existed among us a boy whose mere existence seemed to defy the contours of our collective identity. Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community like a hymn. Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god, he stood in stark contrast to the rest of us, who were more likely to be celebrated for our Talmudic acumen than for any prowess on the athletic field. But there he was, a towering figure of grace and strength, conquering the realms of football, basketball, and baseball with a seeming effortlessness that none of us could emulate. To see him play was to witness something almost sacred, as though the mundane boundaries of our neighborhood had been temporarily lifted to reveal a glimpse of something larger, purer, and profoundly American.We loved him not because he was one of us, but because he was so distinctly other, embodying a kind of transcendence we barely dared to dream of. The Swede was everything we were not allowed to imagine ourselves to be—resilient, fearless, and uncomplicated by the anxieties that knitted themselves into the very fabric of our Jewish existence. To watch him soar above the basketball rim or charge down the football field was to forget, if only for a moment, the war, the ration books, the headlines filled with death. In those fleeting moments, he turned our collective dread into something weightless and buoyant. We made of him an Apollo, a golden boy whose victories on the field were our victories, whose perfection was our imperfect salvation.Even now, I can see him in my mind’s eye, the sunlight catching the blonde halo of his hair as he pitched another strike or sank another jump shot. He was our myth, our impossible hope, the embodiment of a Newark dream in a time when dreaming seemed almost criminal.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: No matter what I thought of myself in childhood, both in times of complimentary self-reference and in self-effacement, I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top. I wasn’t trying to out-duel him, that would have been impossible; it was an effort to get closer to his prestige, even if I could never match it. In Newark nobody did what he did. He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo. With every snap of the bat against the ball, we cheered for him and for our brothers and fathers in the war who might just come home safely if they could channel The Swede’s fiendish affinity for dominant physical triumph, a kind of triumph none of us were used to seeing embodied. He spun through defenders on the basketball court and we imagined Newark’s finest darting through enemy lines toward us. He dove into the opponent’s running back and we imagined our male relatives tackling a Nazi and pounding, pounding, pounding down, breaking them into specific wet bits we could never have seen in such luscious detail otherwise.

He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo.
