written_by_MFA016.Original: The Swede. During the war years, when I was still a grade school boy, this was a magical name in our Newark neighborhood, even to adults just a generation removed from the city's old Prince Street ghetto and not yet so flawlessly Americanized as to be bowled over by the prowess of a high school athlete. The name was magical; so was the anomalous face. Of the few fair-complexioned Jewish students in our preponderantly Jewish public high school, none possessed anything remotely like the steep-jawed, insentient Viking mask of this blue-eyed blond born into our tribe as Seymour Irving Levov.The Swede starred as end in football, center in basketball, and first baseman in baseball. Only the basketball team was ever any good—twice winning the city championship while he was its leading scorer—but as long as the Swede excelled, the fate of our sports teams didn't matter much to a student body whose elders, largely undereducated and overburdened, venerated academic achievement above all else. Physical aggression, even camouflaged by athletic uniforms and official rules and intended to do no harm to Jews, was not a traditional source of pleasure in our community—advanced degrees were. Nonetheless, through the Swede, the neighborhood entered into a fantasy about itself and about the world, the fantasy of sports fans everywhere: almost like Gentiles (as they imagined Gentiles), our families could forget the way things actually work and make an athletic performance the repository of all their hopes. Primarily, they could forget the war.The elevation of Swede Levov into the household Apollo of the Weequahic Jews can best be explained, I think, by the war against the Germans and the Japanese and the fears that it fostered. With the Swede indomitable on the playing field, the meaningless surface of life provided a bizarre, delusionary kind of sustenance, the happy release into a Swedian innocence, for those who lived in dread of never seeing their sons or their brothers or their husbands again.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. Sam, my toddler, doesn't understand why Mommy keeps staring out windows like she's auditioning for a Tennessee Williams play. The truth is, betrayal is a peculiar thing – it doesn't just break your heart, it retrospectively ruins perfectly good memories. Like how that book of children's songs, the one with Thelma's nauseating inscription, has now tainted every lullaby I've ever sung to Sam. The whole thing would be almost comedic if it weren't so tragically predictable – the younger woman, the secret notes, the pregnant wife. It's like someone took every cliché about infidelity and decided to stage it in my living room, with me as the unwitting star of this domestic drama. At least I can say this: nothing makes you reevaluate your life choices quite like finding your husband's mistress's handwriting in your child's bedtime stories.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. When I said it, though, people laughed. Although, now I wonder if they were laughing because it was funny, or because they pitied me. I was certainly quite pitiable.
written_by_MFA001.Reason: I've read this book before so this might affect my perceptions. Both the original and excerpt 2 jump around quite a lot like a stream of consciousness. This shows the narrator's distress. Both the original and excerpt 2 are brutal about Thelma Rice, whereas excerpt 1 does not do this
written_by_MFA001.Original: The first day I did not think it was funny. I didn’t think it was funny the third day either, but I managed to make a little joke about it. “The most unfair thing about this whole business,” I said, “is that I can’t even date.” Well, you had to be there, as they say, because when I put it down on paper it doesn’t sound funny. But what made it funny (trust me) is the word “date,” which when you say it out loud at the end of a sentence has a wonderful teenage quality, and since I am not a teenager (okay, I’m thirty-eight), and since the reason I was hardly in a position to date on first learning that my second husband had taken a lover was that I was seven months pregnant, I got a laugh on it, though for all I know my group was only laughing because they were trying to cheer me up. I needed cheering up. I was in New York, staying in my father’s apartment, I was crying most of the time, and every time I stopped crying I had to look at my father’s incredibly depressing walnut furniture and slate-gray lamps, which made me start crying again.I had gotten on the shuttle to New York a few hours after discovering the affair, which I learned about from a really disgusting inscription to my husband in a book of children’s songs she had given him. Children’s songs. “Now you can sing these songs to Sam” was part of the disgusting inscription, and I can’t begin to tell you how it sent me up the wall, the idea of my two-year-old child, my baby, involved in some dopey inscriptive way in this affair between my husband, a fairly short person, and Thelma Rice, a fairly tall person with a neck as long as an arm and a nose as long as a thumb and you should see her legs, never mind her feet, which are sort of splayed.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.

I didn’t think it was funny the third day either, but I managed to make a little joke about it. “The most unfair thing about this whole business,” I said, “is that I can’t even date.” Well, you had to be there, as they say, because when I put it down on paper it doesn’t sound funny. I needed cheering up. I was in New York, staying in my father’s apartment, I was crying most of the time, and every time I stopped crying I had to look at my father’s incredibly depressing walnut furniture and slate-gray lamps, which made me start crying again.I had gotten on the shuttle to New York a few hours after discovering the affair, which I learned about from a really disgusting inscription to my husband in a book of children’s songs she had given him. Children’s songs. “Now you can sing these songs to Sam” was part of the disgusting inscription, and I can’t begin to tell you how it sent me up the wall, the idea of my two-year-old child, my baby, involved in some dopey inscriptive way in this affair between my husband, a fairly short person, and Thelma Rice, a fairly tall person with a neck as long as an arm and a nose as long as a thumb and you should see her legs, never mind her feet, which are sort of splayed.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I would have gotten him back, I really would, but it’s difficult to date when you’re seven months pregnant. That’s a joke. I’m laughing as I write it. I admit that it feels sad when it’s on paper. The laughter I can hear now is the worst kind: sympathetic laughter. The truth is, I don’t laugh often these days. I cry and cry and cry. I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It’s something you don’t expect from a second husband. Or, I don’t know, maybe you should suspect it more from a second husband. And that name. Thelma Rice. Like a villain in a Roald Dahl book. Imagine my shame, telling people I had been cheated on, at thirty-eight, with a woman named Thelma Rice? I would have gotten him back, I really would, but it’s difficult to date when you’re seven months pregnant. That’s a joke. I’m laughing as I write it. I admit that it feels sad when it’s on paper. The laughter I can hear now is the worst kind: sympathetic laughter. The truth is, I don’t laugh often these days. I cry and cry and cry. I cry in a lot of places, but I do most of my crying in my father’s New York apartment, surrounded by that mocking cuckoo clock and all the uncomfortable plastic furniture. But there is laughter. How can I not laugh when I think of the moment I found out? Sitting on the floor of the nursery, amongst the blocks and the plush toys, cherubic Sam on my knee, opening that children’s song book I found out later was a gift to my husband from Thelma called “The Hungry Hippo.” On the first page, in lascivious handwriting: My darling. Let this be a reminder of how hungry I am for you. xoxo- Thelma. I remember the sound as I snapped the book shut. I remember Sam grabbing for it, wondering why story time was over before it had begun. I can see her when I close my eyes, hunched over that sweet and unassuming book, a hippo herself with that round, smug face, those manly teeth, that grayish skin. To be cheated on when you are seven months pregnant, by your second husband, is one thing. To be cheated on with a woman who resembles a cartoon hippo is entirely another. This, more than anything, is what makes me cry when I’m alone with just my father’s cuckoo clock and the rubber loveseat to keep me company.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.

They only gave you a block or 2 and if you managed to finish, the regular carrier would give you another block to carry, or maybe you'd go back in and the soup would give you another, but you just took your time and shoved those Xmas cards in the slots.I think it was my second day as a Christmas temp that this big woman came out and walked around with me as I delivered letters. What I mean by big was that her ass was big and her tits were big and that she was big in all the right places. She seemed a bit crazy but I kept looking at her body and I didn't care.She talked and talked and talked. Then it came out. Her husband was an officer on an island far away and she got lonely, you know, and lived in this little house in back all by herself."What little house?" I asked.She wrote the address on a piece of paper."I'm lonely too," I said, "I'll come by and we'll talk tonight."I was shacked but the shack job was gone half the time, off somewhere, and I was lonely all right. I was lonely for that big ass standing beside me."All right," she said, "see you tonight."She was a good one all right, she was a good lay but like all lays after the 3rd or 4th night I began to lose interest and didn't go back.But I couldn't help thinking, god, all these mailmen do is drop in their letters and get laid. This is the job for me, oh yes yes yes.”

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I took the job because I needed something easy, something that didn’t ask too many questions, didn’t make me think too hard. A local drunk had mentioned they needed Christmas help at the post office, and that was enough for me. Walk around, dump letters in boxes, pretend to care. Not bad. My second day, I met her—big woman, bigger than me, with those arms that looked like they’d been lifting more than just grocery bags. She stood at the door like she’d been waiting for me all day. “Cold out,” she said, her breath heavy, warm, sweet and rotten at the same time. “Yeah,” I said, “but I don’t mind.” I minded, but I wasn’t about to tell her that. She took the envelope from my hand, but didn’t let go. “Lonely here,” she said. Her husband was stationed somewhere far off, wearing a uniform, probably shining his boots and thinking about her. Poor bastard. “I make good coffee,” she said. That wasn’t coffee she was offering. And I was lonely too, despite having a girl waiting for me somewhere, someone who wasn’t enough, someone who made too much sense. That night, I went back. The place was warm, smelled like burned toast and old carpet. She poured me whiskey instead of coffee, and that was better. We moved from the kitchen to the couch to the bedroom like it was something we’d done before. A few days passed like that. But the thing about loneliness is, it doesn’t go away just because you put your hands on someone. Eventually, the whiskey bottle emptied, the room started feeling smaller, and her laugh turned into something I didn’t want to hear. The job was still there, but the excitement was gone. So I delivered the mail, took my paycheck, and let her find another man to fill the spaces her husband left behind. Being a mailman wasn’t bad. Good work if you like walking. Better work if you don’t mind a little company along the way.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I took the job because I needed something easy, something that didn’t ask too many questions, didn’t make me think too hard. She took the envelope from my hand, but didn’t let go. “Lonely here,” she said. Her husband was stationed somewhere far off, wearing a uniform, probably shining his boots and thinking about her. Poor bastard. “I make good coffee,” she said. That wasn’t coffee she was offering. And I was lonely too, despite having a girl waiting for me somewhere, someone who wasn’t enough, someone who made too much sense. That night, I went back. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: I clutched the bag closer to my chest as the elevator ascended, surrounded by the sterile scents of antiseptic and floor cleaner. A young doctor in a white coat pressed against the back wall, studying a clipboard, while two nurses whispered near the buttons, their voices barely audible above the mechanical hum. The speakers crackled: "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to Ward 3." I watched the numbers illuminate one by one: three, four, five. The bag I had made was perfect—every stitch aligned with precision, the leather supple and warm like living skin. I had spent weeks crafting it, imagining her face when she would first hold it, how her fingers would trace the seams I had sewn with such care. Now it felt heavy in my hands, weighted with purpose, like the shears tucked carefully in my coat pocket. They were old and reliable, the kind my grandmother used for trimming roses, their blades still sharp enough to slice through fabric—or flesh—without resistance. "I've come to show you the modifications I made," I would say, smiling. "See how the clasp catches the light?" She would lean in close, trusting, the way she did before. Her heart would be exposed then, vulnerable beneath her hospital gown. I imagined it beating steadily, unaware of my intentions, like a bird resting in its nest. The elevator chimed for the sixth floor, and I stepped out into the fluorescent-lit corridor. A faint tremor ran through my hands—anticipation, perhaps, or fear. But I knew what I had to do. The bag deserved to be mine alone, freed from her unworthy grasp. I had created it, after all, breathed life into every fold and corner. As I walked toward her room, my footsteps echoing in the empty hallway, I felt a strange calm settle over me. The shears knocked gently against my ribs with each step, a quiet reminder of what was to come.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.

An example would be how the original talks of "the shears in my right pocket prick through my thigh as I wait. The elevator chimes, the number six lights up", and excerpt 2 echoes this with "Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me.". Excerpt 2 has a very similar style that doesn't overdo it's description.
written_by_MFA007.Original: “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Please contact the pharmacy immediately.” The announcement played again, but Dr. Y was apparently still missing.The elevator was crowded with doctors and nurses, and patients with drip bags of yellow liquid, but I forced my way in and pressed the button for the sixth floor. I was sure I’d be able to find her room. I would pretend I was just visiting her, or I could say I wanted her to pay me for the bag. After all, I ought to get something for all my work.First, I’ll apologize for the other day—very humbly, in order to regain her trust. And then I’ll say what I’ve come to say: “Making your bag has been a very important experience for me. I don’t think I’ll ever have the chance to make a piece like this again. Still, I’m happy you’re getting the operation and won’t need the bag. But I do have one final request: I’d like to see it put to its intended use just once. I know it’s asking a lot, but I’d be very grateful. I promise I’ll never bother you again, but nothing is more painful for a craftsman than knowing all his hard work was for nothing. Just this once, and I’d be eternally grateful.”She’ll take off her gown, and I’ll fit it on her.“Are you satisfied, then?” she’ll ask, eager to be rid of me.“Thank you,” I’ll say, but when I reach for the bag, I’ll cut her heart away, too.And then it will be mine alone.The bag is in my left pocket. I tried to fold it flat, but there’s a little mound in my pants. I don’t think anyone will notice. The shears in my right pocket prick my thigh as I wait.The elevator chimes, the number six lights up, and the door opens.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: The elevator hummed its ascent , its metallic echo chamber filled with the rustling of starched white coats and the hushed murmurs of worried voices.  Doctors and nurses, their footsteps brisk and purposeful, pressed against me, their faces etched with lines of clinical concern.  A woman, her hand clutching a crumpled tissue, sobbed softly in the corner, her body trembling with a grief I could not touch.  The tinny voice of the intercom announced, "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine," its monotone a stark contrast to the silent anxieties swirling within the elevator's steel box.I stood amidst this symphony of human emotion, my heart a steady drumbeat against my ribs, my purpose clear.  I was going to see her, the woman who had entrusted me with her memories, her fears, her hopes, woven into the very fabric of the bag I had crafted for her.  I would smile, offer gentle words, tell her how the bag, her bag, was a masterpiece, a testament to her strength, her resilience.  I would ask her to try it on, to feel the weight of it, the way it settled against her, a perfect fit. And then, as her eyes lit up with a flicker of trust, a spark of recognition, I would watch her heart, that fragile vessel of memory, beat against her chest, a tiny bird trapped within a cage of ribs.  I would slice the shears through her skin and cut her heart out. I'd hold her heart in my hands, its warmth a perverse comfort, its rhythm a dark symphony. And then, I'd claim the bag, mine alone, its rightful place by my side, its true purpose fulfilled.The elevator lurched to a halt.The shears lay nestled in my pocket, their sharp blades whispering promises of possession, of a bond that would be mine alone.It was the the sixth floor.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. "Attention: Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, telephone please. Dr. Y, telephone please," a voice over a speaker said. The elevator stopped at last, and I arrived on the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: As the elevator climbed steadily toward the sixth floor, I stood pressed against the cold steel wall, my bag nestled against my side, the shears inside resting unnervingly still. The voice over the intercom announced, “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, please report to ward three,” in a steady monotone, a voice unbothered by the frantic shuffle of nurses and patients around me. The air was tinged with a faint medicinal scent, sharp and sterile, as though the building itself exhaled nothing but clean, cold breath. My thoughts drifted toward her, lying somewhere beyond these walls, fragile and unguarded.The bag felt heavier than it had when I left home, its clasp clicking softly as though whispering to me in a language only it and I could understand. I imagined the look in her eyes as I approached, a flicker of recognition perhaps, then the inevitable softening—a crack in the shield of suspicion she might have built around herself. My words were carefully chosen in advance, rehearsed in the quiet moments of the previous night: admiration for her grace, a humble explanation of my creation, a plea for forgiveness wrapped in layers of calm sincerity.And yet, the weight of the shears burned against the lining of the bag, a cold promise of something darker. The thought of her chest rising and falling, her heart pulsing rhythmically beneath the soft fabric of her gown, stirred a sensation I couldn’t quite place. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I often long to be a better feminist. I know what a good feminist, a correct feminist, looks like. I like wearing pink and scrolling through Pinterest pictures of those 'perfect' women that I know are there to make all us regular women feel terrible about ourselves. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I am a contradiction in motion, a living, breathing paradox who spends far too much time thinking about the ways I fail to measure up to some imagined feminist ideal. There are days when I scroll through Instagram, double-tapping photos of women in impossibly high heels and perfectly curated outfits, while simultaneously drafting tweets about the toxicity of beauty standards. I tell myself I'm participating in critical discourse, but really, I'm just another woman trying to make sense of the impossible space between who I am and who I think I should be. Sometimes I find myself in department stores, running my fingers over silk blouses that cost more than my weekly grocery budget, imagining the kind of woman who wears them—successful, put-together, somehow both feminine and feminist enough. Then I remember how I once wrote a scathing essay about consumerism and capitalism's commodification of feminist empowerment, and I feel like a fraud. But here's the thing: I am tired of apologizing for these contradictions. I am tired of feeling like I need to justify why I can write about dismantling patriarchal beauty standards while also spending forty-five minutes watching makeup tutorials on YouTube. The truth is, I want to be taken seriously as a feminist scholar and intellectual while also wearing sparkly nail polish and watching reality TV shows that probably set feminism back twenty years. I want to rage against the machine while sometimes, just sometimes, finding comfort in the very structures I critique. My feminism lives in this messy middle ground, where theory meets reality, where academic discourse crashes headlong into human desire. I keep thinking about how we're all just trying to navigate this complicated terrain of identity and authenticity, how we're all just fumbling in the dark, reaching for something that feels true. Maybe that's why I find myself drawn to these contradictions—they're the most honest part of who I am. They're the space where my humanity refuses to be neat and tidy, refuses to fit into the boxes we've created for what it means to be a "good" feminist or a "real" woman. So yes, I will continue to critique the patriarchy while also watching "The Bachelor." I will write about intersectional feminism while also obsessing over my skincare routine. I will hold space for all of these seemingly incompatible truths because that's what it means to be human in this complicated, messy world we're trying to change.

There are days when I scroll through Instagram, double-tapping photos of women in impossibly high heels and perfectly curated outfits, while simultaneously drafting tweets about the toxicity of beauty standards. I tell myself I'm participating in critical discourse, but really, I'm just another woman trying to make sense of the impossible space between who I am and who I think I should be. Sometimes I find myself in department stores, running my fingers over silk blouses that cost more than my weekly grocery budget, imagining the kind of woman who wears them—successful, put-together, somehow both feminine and feminist enough. Then I remember how I once wrote a scathing essay about consumerism and capitalism's commodification of feminist empowerment, and I feel like a fraud. But here's the thing: I am tired of apologizing for these contradictions. I am tired of feeling like I need to justify why I can write about dismantling patriarchal beauty standards while also spending forty-five minutes watching makeup tutorials on YouTube. The truth is, I want to be taken seriously as a feminist scholar and intellectual while also wearing sparkly nail polish and watching reality TV shows that probably set feminism back twenty years. I want to rage against the machine while sometimes, just sometimes, finding comfort in the very structures I critique. My feminism lives in this messy middle ground, where theory meets reality, where academic discourse crashes headlong into human desire. I keep thinking about how we're all just trying to navigate this complicated terrain of identity and authenticity, how we're all just fumbling in the dark, reaching for something that feels true. Maybe that's why I find myself drawn to these contradictions—they're the most honest part of who I am. They're the space where my humanity refuses to be neat and tidy, refuses to fit into the boxes we've created for what it means to be a "good" feminist or a "real" woman. written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Instead I found myself nodding slightly to the beat. Because, to tell the truth — it was a catchy tune. Perhaps this makes me a bad feminist. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. I want to be seen, to be loved, even when I can’t love all the parts of myself. And maybe, just maybe, being a bad feminist is better than not trying to be one at all.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Feminism is a complicated thing. It’s a word I wear like an oversized coat, too heavy in some places, too tight in others, but always mine. I say I’m a feminist, but then I catch myself singing along to a rap song where the chorus is basically a hate crime against women. I’ll roll my eyes at beauty standards while simultaneously scrolling through Instagram, obsessing over how that one influencer makes every maxi dress look so effortless. And pink? Don’t even get me started. I own a pink coffee mug that says “Boss Babe” in gold script, which makes me cringe every time I see it, but I still use it every single morning. It’s an emblem of my contradictions, a piece of evidence in the case I’m building against myself.I often wonder if these contradictions make me a bad feminist, a hypocrite. But then I think, isn’t that what being human is? Aren’t we all just patchworks of our contradictions, held together by loose stitches of guilt and self-awareness? I laugh at myself, at my ridiculousness, at how I try to intellectualize everything, including my love of trashy reality TV, which I’ve somehow convinced myself is a feminist act because it’s “women owning their narratives.” That’s bullshit, but it’s my bullshit.I try, in my way, to reconcile these things. I write about them, hoping that if I untangle these thoughts long enough, they’ll make sense, that I’ll make sense. But clarity doesn’t always come, and honestly, I’m not sure I want it to. There’s something freeing about admitting you’re a mess, that you don’t have it all figured out. It’s like stepping off the pedestal before someone else can shove you off.The truth is, I want what I want. I want to be a feminist and a mess. I want to call out misogyny while dancing to songs that degrade women. I want to rage against the patriarchy and wear lipstick that costs more than a week’s worth of groceries. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Boy, it started raining like hell while I watched old Phoebe going around and around on that crazy carousel. I mean it really started coming down, but I didn't give a damn about getting wet. I really didn't. I just stood there with this goofy grin on my face - I probably looked like a complete madman - watching my kid sister in her blue coat having the time of her life. That killed me. It really did. My hunting hat was getting soaked but I didn't care about that either. It's funny, sometimes the things that make you the happiest are the things that get you all sopping wet and probably looking like a complete moron to everybody else. But that's the thing about happiness - it doesn't give a damn what you look like.Now I'm stuck in this crumby place, this rest home or whatever the hell you want to call it, and this hotshot psychoanalyst keeps asking me all these stupid questions about what I'm gonna do with my future. Like if I'm gonna "apply myself" when I go back to school. Jesus Christ, that kills me. These people and their goddam questions. Even old D.B. - he's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still can't help himself. He came to visit me yesterday with this English actress who was sort of beautiful in this fake, Hollywood way. As soon as she went to the bathroom - girls are always going to the bathroom when you're in the middle of something - D.B. starts in with the questions about everything I've been telling him. All about what happened and what I think about it now and all.The funny part is, the more I talk about all this stuff, the more I keep thinking about everybody. Even the people I didn't particularly like, for Chrissake. Like old Stradlater with his secret slob tendencies and Ackley with his pimples and Maurice. I keep thinking about them and missing them, in this crazy way. I don't even know why. I mean, they were all phonies in their own way, but I miss them anyway. That's the thing that drives me crazy in here - how you can hate somebody's guts one minute and then start missing them like hell the next. It's really ironical as hell. Sometimes I think maybe that psychoanalyst isn't so dumb after all, but I'd rather get kicked in the teeth than admit that to him. He'll probably ask me about my violent tendencies next time I see him. That's the trouble with psychoanalysts - they always want to know what everything means, even when things don't mean anything at all.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever. It was coming down in buckets. Even barrels. My hunting hat helped protect my hair a little, but I was soaked all the way to my bones. I didn’t think I’d ever get dry. But even though I was cold and wet, I couldn’t stop feeling so happy that every raindrop was like a miniature sun. I watched Phoebe laughing and waving in her blue coat. She was smiling real big, and after a little while, I realized I was smiling too. The painted horses on the carousel went up and down, and I didn’t want them to ever stop. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. It doesn’t rain very often around here, but when it does, I sit by the windows and remember what it felt like to stand in that crazy downpour. Then I smile just to myself, like a secret. Everybody here asks me the stupidest questions I’ve ever heard. Especially that one doctor. He asked me the other day about whether I plan on applying myself when I go back to school. “That’s none of your goddamn business,” I said to him. “You’re right,” he said. “It isn’t really my business. But it’s your business, isn’t it? Don’t you think your future deserves some consideration?” I told him he was the biggest phony I’d ever met in my life. It probably wasn’t true, but in the moment, it sure felt like it. This doctor keeps telling me I have lots of potential and that if I don’t get better, I’ll waste it. I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. He’s a screenwriter, and not as bad as the other people here, but he still asks lots of questions. Mostly stuff about medicine, which I don’t like talking about, and television, which I’m not even allowed to watch here. The last time he came, he brought along an English actress who wore lots of sparkles. She seemed nervous and kept telling me how brave I was. When she left to go to the bathroom, D.B. asked me what I thought about everything that happened. And I realized that talking about everything made me miss everyone it happened with. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 2 is most similar to the original in terms of voice and style. Both discuss how they feel watching Phoebe go around on the carousel, both described the feeling of speaking with the doctor, and both describe the details of the downpour and how soaked everyone was getting during it.
written_by_MFA029.Original: Boy, it began to rain like a bastard. In buckets, I swear to God. All the parents and mothers and everybody went over and stood right under the roof of the carrousel, so they wouldn’t get soaked to the skin or anything, but I stuck around on the bench for quite a while. I got pretty soaking wet, especially my neck and my pants. My hunting hat really gave me quite a lot of protection, in a way; but I got soaked anyway. I didn’t care, though. I felt so damn happy all of sudden, the way old Phoebe kept going around and around. I was damn near bawling, I felt so damn happy, if you want to know the truth. I don’t know why. It was just that she looked so damn nice, the way she kept going around and around, in her blue coat and all. God, I wish you could’ve been there.That’s all I’m going to tell about. I could probably tell you what I did after I went home, and how I got sick and all, and what school I’m supposed to go to next fall, after I get out of here, but I don’t feel like it. I really don’t. That stuﬀ doesn’t interest me too much right now.A lot of people, especially this one psychoanalyst guy they have here, keeps asking me if I’m going apply myself when I go back to school next September. It’s such a stupid question, in my opinion. I mean how do you know what you’re going to do till you do it? The answer is, you don’t. I think I am, but how do I know? I swear it’s a stupid question. D.B. isn’t as bad as the rest of them, but he keeps asking me a lot of questions, too. He drove over last Saturday with this English babe that’s in this new picture he’s writing. She was pretty aﬀected, but very good-looking. Anyway, one time when she went to the ladies’ room way the hell down in the other wing D.B. asked me what I thought about all this stuﬀ I just ﬁnished telling you about. I didn’t know what the hell to say. If you want to know the truth, I don’t know what I think about it. I’m sorry I told so many people about it. About all I know is, I sort of miss everybody I told about. Even old Stradlater and Ackley, for instance. I think I even miss that goddam Maurice. It’s funny. Don’t ever tell anybody anything. If you do, you start missing everybody.

I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. I got pretty soaking wet, especially my neck and my pants. My hunting hat really gave me quite a lot of protection, in a way; but I got soaked anyway. I didn’t care, though. I felt so damn happy all of sudden, the way old Phoebe kept going around and around. I was damn near bawling, I felt so damn happy, if you want to know the truth. I don’t know why. It was just that she looked so damn nice, the way she kept going around and around, in her blue coat and all. God, I wish you could’ve been there.That’s all I’m going to tell about. I could probably tell you what I did after I went home, and how I got sick and all, and what school I’m supposed to go to next fall, after I get out of here, but I don’t feel like it. I really don’t. That stuﬀ doesn’t interest me too much right now.A lot of people, especially this one psychoanalyst guy they have here, keeps asking me if I’m going apply myself when I go back to school next September. It’s such a stupid question, in my opinion. I mean how do you know what you’re going to do till you do it? The answer is, you don’t. I think I am, but how do I know? I swear it’s a stupid question. D.B. isn’t as bad as the rest of them, but he keeps asking me a lot of questions, too. He drove over last Saturday with this English babe that’s in this new picture he’s writing. She was pretty aﬀected, but very good-looking. Anyway, one time when she went to the ladies’ room way the hell down in the other wing D.B. asked me what I thought about all this stuﬀ I just ﬁnished telling you about. I didn’t know what the hell to say. If you want to know the truth, I don’t know what I think about it. I’m sorry I told so many people about it. About all I know is, I sort of miss everybody I told about. Even old Stradlater and Ackley, for instance. I think I even miss that goddam Maurice. It’s funny. Don’t ever tell anybody anything. If you do, you start missing everybody.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Boy, it was raining like a madman. I mean really coming down. Cats and dogs, like they say. I was watching old Phoebe go around and around on this carousel, and all I could think was, "If only you knew how happy this makes me." She looked so good in that blue coat of hers, just riding that thing like she didn't have a care in the world. Me, I was soaked to the bone. My hunting hat was doing its best, but there's only so much a hat can do when the sky's practically falling down. But I didn't care. I was too busy feeling good to worry about a little rain.You know, it's funny. I'm stuck in this place, and they keep asking me these stupid questions. This one guy, this psychoanalyst or whatever he is, he wants to know if I'm going to apply myself at school. Can you beat that? Like it's the only thing that matters. And then there's old D.B. He's not as bad as the rest of them, but he still asks a lot of questions. He came to see me the other day with this English actress. A real glamour girl, if you know what I mean. Anyway, she went to the bathroom or something, and D.B. starts asking me what I think about all this stuff that's been going on. You know, the stuff I've been telling you about.I don't know why they care so much. It's my life, isn't it? I guess they think they're helping or something. But all they do is make me feel worse. Like I'm some kind of freak show or something. I just wish they'd leave me alone.The thing is, I don't even know what I think myself. It's all so messed up. I mean, I was just telling you about Stradlater and Ackley and Maurice, and now I'm starting to miss those guys. Can you believe that? I didn't even like them that much. But now that I'm not around them anymore, I keep thinking about all the stupid stuff we did together. It's like I'm lonelier now than I was when they were around.I guess that's what this whole thing is about. Loneliness. It's like this big, empty hole inside me that I can't seem to fill. I keep trying to find people to connect with, but it never seems to work out. It's like I'm always looking for something that's not there.Anyway, I'm getting tired of talking about myself. It's boring. Maybe I'll tell you more about old Phoebe sometime. She's a real character, that kid. But for now, I think I'll just sit here and watch the rain. It's kind of peaceful, in a way.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: The rain started a few minutes after Phoebe got on the carousel. It started out light, then almost immediately it began to pour. I mean it was really raining—my shoes started to get soaked, and my hair, but watching her atop the fake little ponies I only felt an overwhelming sense of joy. There was my sister, in her blue coat, laughing and riding on the carousel without a care in the world. I stood there in my soggy shoes for a while just watching her; my hunting hat protected me slightly from the rain, but mostly I didn’t even mind how wet I was getting. I was just so happy watching her there. Really I think that was one of the last times I can remember feeling happy without anything else getting in the way. Later, once I arrived in the facility, I remember the psychoanalyst there asked me some stupid question, something about my future—whether I would start to finally apply myself in school or something. I never knew how to answer dumb questions like that, so usually I’d stay quiet or say something snarky in reply so that they learned to stop asking. Sometimes D.B. would come and see me, which wasn’t so bad, except for the fact that he was always rattling on about his screenwriting career and asking me more stupid questions. “Isn’t there anything you’re passionate about? Anything at all?” I remember once, he came to visit me with this actress woman he had been seeing. She was really glamorous, and I remember she had said she was from England, or maybe I’m just thinking that because she had this snotty-sounding accent. She didn’t really ask me any questions; she mostly just sat there and would speak if D.B. spoke to her. Anyway, there was one time that the two of them came to visit me, and I remember that once the actress went to the bathroom, D.B. leaned in and asked me what I thought of everything that had been going on. “What do you mean?” I asked him, annoyed to have to field yet another question. “I guess I just mean—all of this,” he said, and he stuck his hand out to gesture all around us. I realized then how pointless it had been to share anything with D.B. in the first place, with him or even the one's I didn't like—Stradlater, Ackley, Maurice. I kept thinking that somehow, I’d figure out a way to help them see things the way I did, and then we’d finally understand each other and I wouldn’t have to explain anything anymore. But in the end, all it did was make me feel more alone.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.

My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.
