written_by_MFA029.Original: The news about Walter Berglund wasn’t picked up locally—he and Patty had moved away to Washington two years earlier and meant nothing to St. Paul now—but the urban gentry of Ramsey Hill were not so loyal to their city as not to read the New York Times. According to a long and very unflattering story in the Times, Walter had made quite a mess of his professional life out there in the nation’s capital. His old neighbors had some difficulty reconciling the quotes about him in the Times (“arrogant,” “high-handed,” “ethically compromised”) with the generous, smiling, red-faced 3M employee they remembered pedaling his commuter bicycle up Summit Avenue in February snow; it seemed strange that Walter, who was greener than Greenpeace and whose own roots were rural, should be in trouble now for conniving with the coal industry and mistreating country people. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The irony of Walter's transformation from eco-warrior to coal industry collaborator wasn't lost on the former neighbors in Ramsey Hill, though they nursed their disappointment with the kind of passive-aggressive Midwestern restraint that had always made Patty want to scream into her wine glass. The Times piece had painted him as a sellout, which wasn't exactly wrong but missed the essentially Walter-ish quality of his failure – the way his very righteousness had somehow curdled into its opposite, like milk left too long in a virtuous organic glass bottle. In the early days, watching him pedal off to work on his secondhand Schwinn, his messenger bag stuffed with environmental impact reports and local-economy manifestos, the neighbors had seen him as a kind of secular saint, the sort of man who made them feel better about their own smaller gestures toward planetary salvation. Patty, meanwhile, had performed her own theatre of domestic virtue, pushing that double-wide stroller past crack houses and shuttered storefronts with the kind of aggressive cheer that suggested she was either oblivious to danger or actively courting it. The Victorian they'd bought for a song had been their shared project, their statement of faith in the possibility of redemption – not just of a house or a neighborhood, but of a whole way of life that was vanishing as surely as the ozone layer they worried about while listening to All Things Considered. Every stripped floorboard and replastered wall had seemed to say: See? This is how you do it. This is how you live righteously in a fallen world. But righteousness, it turned out, was a kind of intoxicant, and Walter had drunk deeper than most. The coal deal was just the logical endpoint of his conviction that he alone could save the world – a conviction that had grown more desperate and less discriminating as the world had shown itself increasingly resistant to being saved. The neighbors, sipping their own carefully sourced wine and tending their own carefully curated gardens, could afford to judge him now, secure in the knowledge that they, at least, had never tried quite so hard to be good.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. The Walter Berglund of the New York Times article, the “arrogant” and “ethically compromised” Walter, sounded like a different entity entirely, an evil twin or the result of a personality-altering traumatic brain injury. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: In the quiet confines of Ramsey Hill, the news of Walter Berglund's troubles, as trumpeted by the unforgiving clarion of The New York Times, seemed to echo in a vacuum, its resonance muffled by the simple fact that Walter and Patty had moved to Washington, D.C., two years prior.  It was as if the man portrayed in the article - arrogant, ethically compromised - was a stranger, a doppelganger bearing little resemblance to the Walter they thought they knew.  The Walter they remembered was the lone cyclist, a beacon of environmental idealism in a sea of gas-guzzling SUVs, not someone enmeshed in the murky depths of coal industry dealings.But life, like memory, is a fickle thing, prone to distortions and revisions.  The Berglunds, in their Ramsey Hill days, were pioneers of a sort, young urban homesteaders staking their claim in a neighborhood that had seen better days.  Their Victorian house, a relic of a bygone era, was a testament to their tireless efforts, a monument to sweat equity built amidst the blight of boarded-up windows and rampant vandalism.Patty, a former college athlete, stood out in this gritty landscape, a figure of unflinching resilience pushing her stroller through streets littered with broken glass and the detritus of urban decay.  She was a woman who could change a diaper with one hand while wielding a spackle knife with the other, a woman who could soothe a crying child while simultaneously warding off the advances of an aggressive panhandler.Her days fell into a familiar rhythm: the comforting drone of public radio, the midday reward of a zinfandel, the constant juggling act of motherhood and home renovation.  She was a woman straddling two worlds, one foot planted in the world of middle-class aspirations, the other in the harsh reality of her surroundings. And yet, beneath this veneer of normalcy, there was a hint of vulnerability, a flicker of something unfulfilled.  The Berglunds, for all their outward success, were a study in contrasts, a living embodiment of the American Dream's inherent contradictions.  They were remarkable and yet flawed, their idealism tempered by the compromises and disappointments of life.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.

His old neighbors had some difficulty reconciling the quotes about him in the Times (“arrogant,” “high-handed,” “ethically compromised”) with the generous, smiling, red-faced 3M employee they remembered pedaling his commuter bicycle up Summit Avenue in February snow; it seemed strange that Walter, who was greener than Greenpeace and whose own roots were rural, should be in trouble now for conniving with the coal industry and mistreating country people. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.

written_by_MFA008.Original: The news about Walter Berglund wasn’t picked up locally—he and Patty had moved away to Washington two years earlier and meant nothing to St. Paul now—but the urban gentry of Ramsey Hill were not so loyal to their city as not to read the New York Times. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.

written_by_MFA008.Original: The news about Walter Berglund wasn’t picked up locally—he and Patty had moved away to Washington two years earlier and meant nothing to St. Paul now—but the urban gentry of Ramsey Hill were not so loyal to their city as not to read the New York Times. According to a long and very unflattering story in the Times, Walter had made quite a mess of his professional life out there in the nation’s capital. His old neighbors had some difficulty reconciling the quotes about him in the Times (“arrogant,” “high-handed,” “ethically compromised”) with the generous, smiling, red-faced 3M employee they remembered pedaling his commuter bicycle up Summit Avenue in February snow; it seemed strange that Walter, who was greener than Greenpeace and whose own roots were rural, should be in trouble now for conniving with the coal industry and mistreating country people. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I lay in the hotel bed with Catherine, listening to the rain beat against the windows, and I felt good. Really good. The sheets were cool and smooth, and Catherine's breathing was soft and even beside me, and for the first time in a long while I wasn't alone. Not the way you can be alone in a crowded café or alone in someone else's bed, but really not alone. We didn't need to talk. That was the fine thing about Catherine. You could be quiet with her and it felt right. The rain kept coming down outside and the street lamps made yellow pools on the wet pavement below, and I watched them and felt Catherine's warmth against me, solid and real. I had been with other women before, plenty of them, but it was always like being alone, even when you were holding them. With Catherine it was different. She knew about being alone too, and maybe that's why we could be alone together without it hurting. The world breaks everyone sooner or later, that's what I'd learned. It breaks the brave ones and the gentle ones and even the tough ones who think they can't be broken. But Catherine and I, we were already broken when we found each other, so maybe that's why we fit. We didn't need to pretend. The rain was coming down harder now, drumming against the roof, and Catherine stirred beside me but didn't wake. I looked at her face in the dim light and thought about how the world would try to break us too, the way it breaks everything good and true. But for now we had this - the rain outside and the warm bed and the knowledge that we weren't alone. Sometimes that's all you get in this world, these small moments of peace before the breaking starts again. But maybe if you're lucky, you find someone who knows how to pick up the pieces with you. Catherine knew about pieces. She knew about breaking. And here in this room, with the rain coming down, we had put our broken pieces together and made something whole.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: We looked around the hotel room when we opened the door. To be away together! Catherine’s arm looped around my shoulders with mine around her waist. She’d been clearer to me than myself, because I didn’t spend all day studying myself the way I spent all day studying her. My investigation was not complete. We made drinks and sat in the corner chairs. It didn’t matter much that we hadn’t been in the room before. A sense of being at home, of familiarity, accompanied me with Catherine wherever we went together. Rain came down outside in long slants and we listened to the sound in between our conversations and during our sips of drink. The glasses emptied and we filled them up. We could sit in silence, alone with our thoughts but connected somehow. There was the pleasure of watching another think without fear of being caught. She might have even had the expectation of me watching her think. With others long moments of silence had an itchy quality. With friends and lovers I had clawed back into conversation when it faltered or ended naturally. This time as we lay in bed gazing around at the room my mind wandered to those distant relationships and those people who hadn’t met someone like Catherine. Perhaps many people had never experienced a companionship of this magnitude. The magnitude of an arm or a leg. When we made it to the bed we were welcomed by smooth silk sheets that only enhanced the sense of our comfort together, reunited. I reached out and touched her skin and watched my finger trace a white line down her shoulder. A melancholy settled over me. The nature of the world when taken without this comfort breaks everyone and kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. Perhaps those who suffer this fate can persevere for a time or recover from its cruelty in short bursts. Still, suffer they will. When I looked back at her face, which had landed on the warm ball of light atop the lamp, I felt a special kind of fear.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: The original is quite a 'flowing' piece of text that is both descriptive and poetic. The first excerpt is the closest of the two, and matches the original style fairly well. The second excerpt feels more "first person", feels overly emotional and somewhat more excitable in style than the original.
written_by_MFA016.Original: That night at the hotel, in our room with the long empty hall outside and our shoes outside the door, a thick carpet on the floor of the room, outside the windows the rain falling and in the room light and pleasant and cheerful, then the light out and it exciting with smooth sheets and the bed comfortable, feeling that we had come home, feeling no longer alone, waking in the night to find the other one there, and not gone away; all other things were unreal. We slept when we were tired and if we woke the other one woke too so one was not alone. Often a man wishes to be alone and a girl wishes to be alone too and if they love each other they are jealous of that in each other, but I can truly say we never felt that. We could feel alone when we were together, alone against the others. It has only happened to me like that once. I have been alone while I was with many girls and that is the way that you can be most lonely. But we were never lonely and never afraid when we were together.I know that the night is not the same as the day: that all things are different, that the things of the night cannot be explained in the day, because they do not then exist, and the night can be a dreadful time for lonely people once their loneliness has started. But with Catherine there was almost no difference in the night except that it was an even better time. If people bring so much courage to this world the world has to kill them to break them, so of course it kills them. The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.

I could hear the water in the street below, the hush of tires passing, the occasional step of someone hurrying through the wet. It was a good sound. It made the room feel safer. I turned my head and looked at her. Her hair was against her cheek, and I wanted to brush it away, but I didn’t. There was time for that. There was time for everything now, and it felt like all the time in the world.She stirred but did not wake. I watched her for a while. I had been alone before. I had lain in beds in places that were not home, in cities where the streets ran like rivers and the lights burned cold and far away, and I had felt the loneliness of it even with someone there. But not with her. That was the difference. With her, even silence felt full. We could sit in it, breathe in it, and nothing would press between us. It was something rare, something I had not known before. I had known plenty of other things. The empty hours in cafés, the taste of bad brandy, the way a night could stretch and break you down. I had known the sound of laughter that didn’t belong to me, and the way people looked past you when they didn’t want to see. But this was different.Outside, the rain did not stop. It never did. The world went on breaking people, wearing them down like stone in a river, like wood left too long in the salt and the sun. It broke the best first, the gentle ones, the ones who carried too much in them. The others it let last longer, but not forever. No one lasted forever. But for now, for this moment, there was just the quiet, the warmth of the sheets, the softness of her breath, and the rain against the glass.
written_by_MFA009.Reason: The second one is better. It also has a pretentious and almost unreadable tone to it. The "thing of the night that cannot be explained in the day" is comparable to "laughter that didn't belong to me." They are both bad writing that makes reader struggle to understand what the author meant to say.
written_by_MFA009.Original: That night at the hotel, in our room with the long empty hall outside and our shoes outside the door, a thick carpet on the floor of the room, outside the windows the rain falling and in the room light and pleasant and cheerful, then the light out and it exciting with smooth sheets and the bed comfortable, feeling that we had come home, feeling no longer alone, waking in the night to find the other one there, and not gone away; all other things were unreal. We slept when we were tired and if we woke the other one woke too so one was not alone. Often a man wishes to be alone and a girl wishes to be alone too and if they love each other they are jealous of that in each other, but I can truly say we never felt that. We could feel alone when we were together, alone against the others. It has only happened to me like that once. I have been alone while I was with many girls and that is the way that you can be most lonely. But we were never lonely and never afraid when we were together.I know that the night is not the same as the day: that all things are different, that the things of the night cannot be explained in the day, because they do not then exist, and the night can be a dreadful time for lonely people once their loneliness has started. But with Catherine there was almost no difference in the night except that it was an even better time. If people bring so much courage to this world the world has to kill them to break them, so of course it kills them. The world breaks every one and afterward many are strong at the broken places. But those that will not break it kills. It kills the very good and the very gentle and the very brave impartially. If you are none of these you can be sure it will kill you too but there will be no special hurry.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: I spent the night with Catherine in our hotel room overlooking the little square with the rain coming down outside, our bodies naked under the sheets, and the sheets were smooth cotton, and they were good sheets, and I told Catherine so, and she put her feet between my bare legs, and her feet were cold but soon they became warm, and I put my fingers between her hair, and it felt like we were at home together, and I told her so. She smiled and looked at the rain trickle down the glass of the window, and I knew I did not need to say anything else about that.  Because she understood, unlike so many others who I've sought to find and spend time with, who I thought understood and did not, and when I tried to be together with them, our togetherness was lonelier than our solitude. With Catherine, in our togetherness we were solitary still. We held each other up and made each other feel courage in mutual independence. She kissed my cheek, and I looked up at the light on the ceiling, which was turned off, but I could see the streetlights reflect into it through the window. Just the barest bit of light there in the glass, and I thought of how fragile it all was, because this is not a world for rareness. It is a harsh world which breaks everyone, especially the very good and the very gentle and the very brave. It rises to break them all the more, and the more bravery and goodness and gentleness it is met with, the more harshness it responds with. I put my hand on Catherine's shoulder, and I felt the warmth there, and I wondered whether warmth existed because of cold or cold because of warmth. If it was a cold world, as it was a harsh one, what it meant that our bodies were warm when we lived and cold when we died. I thought there was no way to stay warm forever. No matter how long we held each other, the cold still eventually came.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The club's mahogany-paneled dining room felt both intimate and imposing, much like the billionaire himself who sat across from me in his unexpectedly casual attire - a contradiction that seemed to epitomize the entire encounter. He spoke of his software project with the same blithe enthusiasm one might discuss a hobby, though its purpose - to predict employee betrayal - carried an unmistakable darkness beneath its technological sheen. I found myself watching his hands as he gestured, noting how they moved with the unrestrained energy of someone unaccustomed to constraint, while waitresses appeared and disappeared around us like temporal markers, each bringing increasingly elaborate dishes that created their own kind of narrative. The literary magazine, ostensibly the reason for our meeting, seemed to float between us as an abstraction, less substantial than the wine being continuously poured into our glasses. When he mentioned his floating wind farm, complete with worker housing, I recognized in his tone the particular cadence of someone who had grown accustomed to reshaping reality according to their whims - a power that seemed to have preserved in him something childlike, even as it had presumably destroyed other, more ordinary qualities. The adopted Guatemalan quadruplets entered the conversation with the same matter-of-factness as his rock band drumming, both details that seemed to resist integration into any coherent whole. Throughout lunch, I felt myself becoming increasingly passive, as though I were merely a surface upon which his life story was being projected - his humble beginnings, his current affluence, his schemes to eliminate lawyers from personal matters - all of it washing over me in waves that left me struggling to maintain my own sense of reality. When he finally deposited me in the taxi with a casual "Enjoy yourself in Athens" - a destination I was certain I hadn't mentioned - I felt as though I had experienced something that existed outside the normal boundaries of social interaction, an encounter that had its own internal logic but one that, like his software, seemed designed to predict something I couldn't quite grasp.

The tone is more logical, distant and serious which is the same. In excerpt one parts of it are relayed through the voice of the billionaire :'he said...' which is not how it comes across in the original piece.
written_by_MFA007.Original: Before the flight I was invited for lunch at a London club with a billionaire I’d been promised had liberal credentials. He talked in his open-necked shirt about the new software he was developing, that could help organisations identify the employees most likely to rob and betray them in the future. We were meant to be discussing a literary magazine he was thinking of starting up: unfortunately I had to leave before we arrived at that subject. He insisted on paying for a taxi to the airport, which was useful since I was late and had a heavy suitcase.The billionaire had been keen to give me the outline of his life story, which had begun unprepossessingly and ended – obviously – with him being the relaxed, well-heeled man who sat across the table from me today. I wondered whether in fact what he wanted now was to be a writer, with the literary magazine as his entrée. A lot of people want to be writers: there was no reason to think you couldn’t buy your way into it. This man had bought himself in, and out, of a great many things. He mentioned a scheme he was working on, to eradicate lawyers from people’s personal lives. He was also developing a blueprint for a floating wind farm big enough to accommodate the entire community of people needed to service and run it: the gigantic platform could be located far out to sea, thus removing the unsightly turbines from the stretch of coast where he was hoping to pilot the proposal and where, incidentally, he owned a house. On Sundays he played drums in a rock band, just for fun. He was expecting his eleventh child, which wasn’t as bad as it sounded when you considered that he and his wife had once adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. I was finding it difficult to assimilate everything I was being told. The waitresses kept bringing more things, oysters, relishes, special wines. He was easily distracted, like a child with too many Christmas presents. But when he put me in the taxi he said, enjoy yourself in Athens, though I didn’t remember telling him that was where I was going.

I found myself watching his hands as he gestured, noting how they moved with the unrestrained energy of someone unaccustomed to constraint, while waitresses appeared and disappeared around us like temporal markers, each bringing increasingly elaborate dishes that created their own kind of narrative. The literary magazine, ostensibly the reason for our meeting, seemed to float between us as an abstraction, less substantial than the wine being continuously poured into our glasses. When he mentioned his floating wind farm, complete with worker housing, I recognized in his tone the particular cadence of someone who had grown accustomed to reshaping reality according to their whims - a power that seemed to have preserved in him something childlike, even as it had presumably destroyed other, more ordinary qualities. The adopted Guatemalan quadruplets entered the conversation with the same matter-of-factness as his rock band drumming, both details that seemed to resist integration into any coherent whole. Throughout lunch, I felt myself becoming increasingly passive, as though I were merely a surface upon which his life story was being projected - his humble beginnings, his current affluence, his schemes to eliminate lawyers from personal matters - all of it washing over me in waves that left me struggling to maintain my own sense of reality. When he finally deposited me in the taxi with a casual "Enjoy yourself in Athens" - a destination I was certain I hadn't mentioned - I felt as though I had experienced something that existed outside the normal boundaries of social interaction, an encounter that had its own internal logic but one that, like his software, seemed designed to predict something I couldn't quite grasp.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?
written_by_MFA007.Reason: This feels like it was written by Rachel Cusk. Excerpt 1 does a better job at conveying the original's laize-faire type indifference to the onslaught of wealth on display. Meanwhile, excerpt 2 seems like a cloying copy of the original. Especially it ending with the godawful question mark for a statement, not a question.
written_by_MFA007.Original: Before the flight I was invited for lunch at a London club with a billionaire I’d been promised had liberal credentials. He talked in his open-necked shirt about the new software he was developing, that could help organisations identify the employees most likely to rob and betray them in the future. We were meant to be discussing a literary magazine he was thinking of starting up: unfortunately I had to leave before we arrived at that subject. He insisted on paying for a taxi to the airport, which was useful since I was late and had a heavy suitcase.The billionaire had been keen to give me the outline of his life story, which had begun unprepossessingly and ended – obviously – with him being the relaxed, well-heeled man who sat across the table from me today. I wondered whether in fact what he wanted now was to be a writer, with the literary magazine as his entrée. A lot of people want to be writers: there was no reason to think you couldn’t buy your way into it. This man had bought himself in, and out, of a great many things. He mentioned a scheme he was working on, to eradicate lawyers from people’s personal lives. He was also developing a blueprint for a floating wind farm big enough to accommodate the entire community of people needed to service and run it: the gigantic platform could be located far out to sea, thus removing the unsightly turbines from the stretch of coast where he was hoping to pilot the proposal and where, incidentally, he owned a house. On Sundays he played drums in a rock band, just for fun. He was expecting his eleventh child, which wasn’t as bad as it sounded when you considered that he and his wife had once adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. I was finding it difficult to assimilate everything I was being told. The waitresses kept bringing more things, oysters, relishes, special wines. He was easily distracted, like a child with too many Christmas presents. But when he put me in the taxi he said, enjoy yourself in Athens, though I didn’t remember telling him that was where I was going.

Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.

written_by_MFA029.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.

I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.

written_by_MFA029.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south. It stole through the village like a hungry ghost, leaving empty spaces where laughter and life once thrived. Then came the long walk westward, the elders leaning heavily on their canes, the children clinging to their mothers’ skirts. We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. The government men came again, their words like sharp stones cutting through our hearts. Exile. Loss. Land stolen, not by force, but by the stroke of a pen on official documents.In 1914, a new sickness arrived, a slow, insidious cough that consumed the lungs and the spirit. Consumption, they called it. It spread through the reservation like wildfire, leaving behind a trail of sorrow and empty beds. The Pillagers, huddled close in their crowded homes, succumbed one by one. My family, my friends, my neighbors, all taken by the relentless disease. I watched them go, helpless to stop the tide of grief that threatened to drown me.And then, there was only me. Nanapush, the last of his line, an elder at fifty, my hair prematurely streaked with the white of winter. I led the last buffalo hunt, the thundering hooves echoing through the vast emptiness of the plains. I saw the last bear fall. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last old birch tree, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind.But even in the face of such overwhelming loss, I found the strength to resist. I saved the last of the Pillager family, their faces etched with the same sorrow that mirrored my own. I refused to sign the government papers, those insidious documents that would erase us, make us invisible in our own land.

We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. The government men came again, their words like sharp stones cutting through our hearts. Exile. Loss. Land stolen, not by force, but by the stroke of a pen on official documents.In 1914, a new sickness arrived, a slow, insidious cough that consumed the lungs and the spirit. Consumption, they called it. It spread through the reservation like wildfire, leaving behind a trail of sorrow and empty beds. The Pillagers, huddled close in their crowded homes, succumbed one by one. My family, my friends, my neighbors, all taken by the relentless disease. I watched them go, helpless to stop the tide of grief that threatened to drown me.And then, there was only me. Nanapush, the last of his line, an elder at fifty, my hair prematurely streaked with the white of winter. I led the last buffalo hunt, the thundering hooves echoing through the vast emptiness of the plains. I saw the last bear fall. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last old birch tree, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind.But even in the face of such overwhelming loss, I found the strength to resist. I saved the last of the Pillager family, their faces etched with the same sorrow that mirrored my own. I refused to sign the government papers, those insidious documents that would erase us, make us invisible in our own land.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_MFA007.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer in voice style and phrase of the paragraph, excerpts 1 captured the intent of the original paragraph will add it's own additional words to it with the intent of providing more context to the text for better understanding, where as, excerpt 2  use it own words and meaning to describe the original paragraph.
written_by_MFA007.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In the damp quiet of that reservation, I stood as the last thread holding together the vast, frayed tapestry of our people, the Anishinabe. Sickness had come, spotted and relentless, rising from the south to crawl across our bodies, marking us for the grave. We fled westward, believing Dakota land might swallow us whole and offer peace, only to be met with treaties that tangled words into chains we could never untether. The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: You fucked up, straight up. No way to pretty it up with words your fancy-ass MFA taught you—fifty mujeres over six years, all those emails stacked up like bodies, like evidence in one of them CSI episodes your girl used to love watching with you on the couch, back when she thought you were something else, something better, something more than just another Dominican tigre con su vaina. Your bad-ass salcedense who survived the Bar exam like a warrior, who held your hand through all your broke-ass teaching days eating mangú for dinner three times a week, who cried against your shoulder when her pops passed—she warned your ass about cheating, told you straight up how her old man did her mom dirty, how that shit was unforgivable, how it lived in her bones like a curse. But you did it anyway, thinking you were too smooth to get caught, thinking them delete buttons would save your ass forever, thinking you had some special blessing from Ochún herself. Then comes the fucking emails, each one like a bullet, like them killing blows they teach you about in them martial arts movies. Your girl, she give you them three extra months though—three months of plane rides and hotel rooms, three months of you watching her turn into somebody else, somebody with eyes that looked right through you like you was a ghost. In New Zealand, watching her walking that beach she dreamed about since forever, since that movie with the piano, you knew it was done. She wouldn't let you touch her, wouldn't let you near. Y'all drove past some happy-ass couple all wrapped up in each other and the silence in that rental car could've drowned a thousand islands. Later in the hotel room, when she finally broke down, tears coming like they'd never stop, you knew: some things you break, they don't never get fixed. Some betrayals cut too deep for even the ocean to wash away.
