written_by_MFA015.Original: Your girl catches you cheating. (Well, actually she’s your fiancée, but hey, in a bit it so won’t matter.) She could have caught you with one sucia, she could have caught you with two, but because you’re a totally batshit cuero who never empties his e-mail trash can, she caught you with fifty! Sure, over a six-year period, but still. Fifty fucking girls? God damn! Maybe if you’d been engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita you could have survived it—but you’re not engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita. Your girl is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn’t believe in open anything; in fact, the one thing she warned you about, that she swore she would never forgive, was cheating. I’ll put a machete in you, she promised. And, of course, you swore you wouldn’t do it. You swore you wouldn’t. You swore you wouldn’t.And you did.She’ll stick around for a few months because you been together a long, long time. Because you’ve gone through so much together—her father’s death, your tenure madness, her bar exam (passed on the third attempt). And because love, real love, is not so easily shed. Over a tortured six-month period you fly together to the D.R., to Mexico (for the funeral of a friend), to New Zealand. You walk the beach where they filmed “The Piano,” something she’s always wanted to do, and now, in penitent desperation, you give it to her. She is immensely sad on that beach and she walks up and down the shining sand alone, her bare feet in the freezing water, and when you try to hug her she says, Don’t. She stares at the rocks jutting out of the water, the wind carrying her hair straight back. On the ride out to the hotel, up through those wild steeps, you pick up a pair of hitchhikers, a couple so giddy with love that you almost throw them out of the car. She says nothing. Later, in the hotel, she cries.

Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: You’ve been cheating on your fiance, a bad-ass salcedense from the DR who by all accounts doesn’t deserve it. Why? And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.

Your bad-ass salcedense fiancée, the one whose father you'd helped bury, whose law school dreams you'd supported, whose hand you'd held through the darkest nights, now stared at you with an emptiness that mirrored the hollow in your own chest.She didn't leave right away.  Maybe it was the years woven together, the memories of her father's funeral, the echo of your own failures, the triumph of her passing the bar.  You clung to those shared moments like a life raft in a sea of your own making.You tried to mend the shattered pieces with trips – the Dominican Republic, Mexico, even the beach in New Zealand she'd dreamed of since "The Piano."  But on that windswept shore, her sadness was a tangible thing, a wall you couldn't breach.  She walked alone, the sand stretching out like a metaphor for the distance between you.In the rental car, a giddy couple, their love a bright, painful contrast, drove past, and you saw the reflection of your guilt in her eyes.  Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. You remembered her fierce independence, her unwavering loyalty, the way she could light up a room with her smile.  And you had dimmed that light, extinguished it with your own selfishness.You had broken the trust that had been the foundation of your relationship, and the cracks were irreparable.  The guilt gnawed at you, a constant reminder of the pain you had caused.  You had betrayed the woman you loved, and the consequences were devastating.

written_by_MFA006.Original: Your girl catches you cheating. (Well, actually she’s your fiancée, but hey, in a bit it so won’t matter.) She could have caught you with one sucia, she could have caught you with two, but because you’re a totally batshit cuero who never empties his e-mail trash can, she caught you with fifty! Sure, over a six-year period, but still. Fifty fucking girls? God damn! Maybe if you’d been engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita you could have survived it—but you’re not engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita. Your girl is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn’t believe in open anything; in fact, the one thing she warned you about, that she swore she would never forgive, was cheating. I’ll put a machete in you, she promised. And, of course, you swore you wouldn’t do it. You swore you wouldn’t. You swore you wouldn’t.And you did.She’ll stick around for a few months because you been together a long, long time. Because you’ve gone through so much together—her father’s death, your tenure madness, her bar exam (passed on the third attempt). And because love, real love, is not so easily shed. Over a tortured six-month period you fly together to the D.R., to Mexico (for the funeral of a friend), to New Zealand. You walk the beach where they filmed “The Piano,” something she’s always wanted to do, and now, in penitent desperation, you give it to her. She is immensely sad on that beach and she walks up and down the shining sand alone, her bare feet in the freezing water, and when you try to hug her she says, Don’t. She stares at the rocks jutting out of the water, the wind carrying her hair straight back. On the ride out to the hotel, up through those wild steeps, you pick up a pair of hitchhikers, a couple so giddy with love that you almost throw them out of the car. She says nothing. Later, in the hotel, she cries.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: You’ve been cheating on your fiance, a bad-ass salcedense from the DR who by all accounts doesn’t deserve it. Why? Because you’re some sort of idiot hijo de cuero, but you knew that about yourself long before she found the emails. Fifty women jammed into six years–it’s almost impressive, when you think about it. Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The wine had softened the edges of her caution, and Ifemelu found herself speaking with the kind of raw honesty that would later keep her awake at night. "You want to know about being black in America?" she said, watching the poet across the table touch her water glass nervously. "I'll tell you something nobody says at these nice dinner parties. In Nigeria, I was just me. Then I came to America and became black, and suddenly everything changed. Even love changed." She paused, feeling Blaine's eyes on her, his expression unreadable in that way that meant he was already preparing for the aftermath of her words. "You talk about progress, about how interracial marriage is legal now, as if I should be grateful for permission to love. But let me tell you what it's really like. It's lying awake at night, next to someone you love, wondering if you should mention the casual racism at his family dinner. It's smiling when his friends make those little jokes, those little slips, because you don't want to be that angry Black woman who can't take a joke. It's watching him discover racism like it's a new thing, while you've been carrying it on your back since the day you landed in this country." The Frenchwoman's husband shifted in his chair, his liberal discomfort a familiar sight, but Ifemelu pressed on, the truth spilling out like wine on white tablecloth. "And the intimacy, oh, the intimacy is the worst part. Because in bed, in the dark, you wonder – does he see my skin? Does he see past it? And which would be worse?" She laughed, a sound with edges sharp enough to cut. "Then there's the performance of it all, ndi oma. The nice progressive couple at the farmer's market, at gallery openings, at dinner parties like this one, where everyone pretends we're all the same underneath, where I must be just Black enough to be interesting but not enough to make anyone uncomfortable." The other guests leaned forward, titillated by her frankness, as though she were telling them gossip instead of truth. She could feel tomorrow's regret already forming, but the wine urged her forward, made her bold and reckless. "Should I tell you about Curt?" she asked, watching the poet's bangles jingle with anxiety. "Now that's a story about race in America."
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: "It means something different, to be Black here. Something wide and heavy, and I wasn't expecting that, when I moved. You can meet someone, and they can seem perfect for you. But if they're white - when you go outside, that's all anyone cares about. Their whiteness, your Blackness. And you have to dodge the dirty looks people give you on the street. And if you want to talk about that, with your partner - suddenly you're the bad guy. You can't bring up how racism makes you feel because all of a sudden they're defensive and angry, they think you're calling them a racist. And they can't understand, really, what it feels like to be looked at the way people sometimes look at me. Like I'm nothing, or less than nothing." As Ifemelu spoke, Blaine's lips were pressing into a thin, straight line. He looked studiously at his fork, refusing to meet her eyes. A part of her brain cautioned her to stop talking, but the wine had made her tongue heavy and her jaw loose. "People are always saying to me - fifty years ago, you would have been locked up if you tried to date a white man, look at how far this country has come! That's all people ever want to talk about, how much progress has been made. Everyone expects me to be so grateful and happy to be here, but all I can think about is how awful it feels sometimes, to live here and always be thinking about how other people are seeing me." Ifemelu paused. Her own words were echoing in her ears, and she felt the stinging truth of them. The poet seized upon this break and pointed down at his plate. "How did you make these Brussels sprouts?" he said, and the French host seemed not to hear him at all; her eyes were trained on Ifemelu. "But why so pessimistic?" she asked, almost breathlessly, leaning in like Ifemelu was delivering scandalous gossip. "Maybe the people in your past were just wrong for you in some way. Maybe they're skewing your perception." Ifemelu drained the rest of her glass and tightened her fingers around the stem. "The people in my past didn't skew my perception - they showed me the truth," Ifemelu said bitterly. "Let me tell you about this one man I used to date - his name was Curt."

written_by_MFA001.Original: "The only reason you say that race was not an issue is because you wish it was not. We all wish it was not. But it’s a lie. I came from a country where race was not an issue; I did not think of myself as black and I only became black when I came to America. When you are black in America and you fall in love with a white person, race doesn’t matter when you’re alone together because it’s just you and your love. But the minute you step outside, race matters. But we don’t talk about it. We don’t even tell our white partners the small things that piss us off and the things we wish they understood better, because we’re worried they will say we’re overreacting, or we’re being too sensitive. And we don’t want them to say, Look how far we’ve come, just forty years ago it would have been illegal for us to even be a couple blah blah blah, because you know what we’re thinking when they say that? We’re thinking why the fuck should it ever have been illegal anyway? But we don’t say any of this stuff. We let it pile up inside our heads and when we come to nice liberal dinners like this, we say that race doesn’t matter because that’s what we’re supposed to say, to keep our nice liberal friends comfortable. It’s true. I speak from experience." The host, a Frenchwoman, glanced at her American husband, a slyly pleased smile on her face; the most unforgettable dinner parties happened when guests said unexpected, and potentially offensive, things.The poet shook her head and said to the host, “I’d love to take some of that wonderful dip home if you have any left,” and looked at the others as though she could not believe they were actually listening to Ifemelu. But they were, all of them hushed, their eyes on Ifemelu as though she was about to give up a salacious secret that would both titillate and implicate them. Ifemelu had been drinking too much white wine; from time to time she had a swimming sensation in her head, and she would later send apology e-mails to the host and the poet. But everyone was watching her, even Blaine, whose expression she could not, for once, read clearly. And so she began to talk about Curt.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: "It's amazing, how the same things that happen between a man and a woman can be so different simply because of their race." She paused, swirling the wine in her glass, the crystal catching the light. "Before I came here, I never really thought of myself as Black." The table, a mix of faces, both familiar and new, leaned in, intrigued. "But here, suddenly, I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm a Black woman dating a white man." She let out a small, humorless laugh. "It's like this whole other layer gets added, this… awareness, this constant hum in the background that you can't quite ignore." "But things are so much better now, no?" The Frenchwoman, her accent a delicate lilt, tilted her head. "You couldn't even… you know…" she trailed off, gesturing vaguely. "Marry each other?" She finished for her, feeling the familiar sting. "Yes, we've 'progressed.' Now we can be together, but we still have to tiptoe around all the unspoken things." She took another sip, the wine warming her throat, loosening her tongue. "Like, I can't get too angry, can't disagree too strongly, because then I'm not just Ifemelu, I'm the angry Black woman." "Oh, but that's…" the poet, his brow furrowed, shifted uncomfortably. "I mean, surely, it's not…" "Food's getting cold, don't you think?" Blaine, ever the diplomat, interjected smoothly. But she was on a roll, the words tumbling out, fueled by the wine and years of unspoken frustrations. "And it's not just him, it's everyone. This constant… need to remind me how far we've come. As if I should be grateful." She looked around the table, their faces a mixture of fascination and discomfort. "You know, 'Remember when you couldn't even have a drink at the same bar?' As if that somehow makes everything okay now." "But…" the poet started, but she cut him off. "It's like this weird performance, you know? Always being aware of how I'm perceived, what I represent." She met Blaine's eyes across the table, his expression unreadable. "And sometimes, I want to… scream, to break free from this invisible script that everyone seems to have for me." A heavy silence settled over the table. She knew she was oversharing, knew she'd regret this in the morning. But tonight, the wine had given her a voice, a raw, unfiltered voice. "Like with Curt, for example…" she began, feeling a new wave of memories, a new wave of honesty, washing over her.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Ifemelu looks at her Frenchwoman host and her American husband, both grinning with rows of straight teeth, and puts down her wine glass. The wine loosens her tongue and she cannot help it when she says, "America is obsessed with race. I never realized how much until I moved here and now I can't get away from it." She speaks quickly, the words coming easily to her despite the many eyes now firmly fixed on her. With her captive audience, she could almost be a college professor, the kind that reminds her of cult leaders. The watching usually makes her skin crawl, but now it feels like the eyes are attached to ears that are earnestly listening. She tells them that every time she goes outside, she is acutely aware of her blackness in a way she has never experienced before. "Because I'm so aware," she says, "I'm extra-aware when I'm with a boyfriend. And it's not just me, it's everyone in an interracial relationship! You don't want your boyfriend accusing you of being too sensitive, you know? Men always call women crybabies, so you don't want him thinking you're any more emotional than he already believes. Confirmation bias! So you pretend it doesn't bother you, even though it really does. And you can't complain to anyone else about your white boyfriend, either, because there's always some old crone muttering about how, well," she pitches her voice for a biting mimicry. "Interracial relationships used to be illegal, which is so infantilizing to point out! Just because things used to be worse, doesn't mean I can't be frustrated by them still being bad!" she says, and she looks at her nice, liberal audience, and how they've all put down their forks as if eating would mean they aren't listening. They're leaning forward, watching her like a specimen under a microscope. Her hosts are chuckling to each other, but nodding along. Next to them, the poet, who has been a far quieter guest than Ifemelu, tugs at the Frenchwoman's sleeve to nervously compliment one of the side dishes. She absently thanks him and gestures for Ifemelu to keep going. Blaine's face is shuttered, and Ifemelu takes another sip of wine. Distantly, she thinks she might regret this tomorrow. She opens her mouth, though, and says, "It was like that with my ex-boyfriend, Curt." Blaine's lip twitches. Ifemelu says, "He just couldn't understand."

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1:
You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. You know," Ifemelu said, pausing just long enough to sip from her wine glass, the red liquid pooling against her lips before she swallowed, "America is a country where you don't realize you're Black until you’re already inside it, moving through it, breathing it. And then, suddenly, you are." She looked at the poet, the one with the too-smooth bald head and the vaguely British accent that made him sound more thoughtful than he really was. He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. As if race is a scarf you can slip off when you’re with someone who loves you. But it’s always there, waiting, pressing against your throat."  

The Frenchwoman, her teeth unnaturally white, gave a performative sigh. "But we have made such progress, no? Fifty years ago, interracial love was illegal!"  

Ifemelu laughed, a dry, humorless sound. "And what am I supposed to do with that? Be grateful? Tell myself I am lucky that I can now hold my white boyfriend’s hand in public without being arrested? That’s like telling me I should celebrate because women can now vote. It's not a gift. It's not progress. It's just removing something that should never have been there to begin with."  

The poet, desperate now, reached for his fork, stabbing aimlessly at the roasted carrots on his plate. "This is delicious," he muttered, and Ifemelu almost felt sorry for him, because what else was he supposed to say?  

"Race in America is like the weather," she said. "You can pretend it's not there, pretend that the sun is shining, but at some point, it will rain. And when it does, some of us will have umbrellas, and some of us will just get wet."  

A silence settled, the kind that stretched and pulled, thick with the weight of something unspoken. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. And when she said, almost offhandedly, "Curt used to say he didn’t see color," she knew she was not finished yet.

He shifted in his seat. She had said something that made him uncomfortable, which meant she had said something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. Ifemelu glanced at Blaine, saw the way his jaw was set, and knew there would be a conversation later. Maybe an argument. Maybe a quiet, careful "I think you were too harsh." But for now, she felt the soft, warm buzz of the wine, the thrill of having said something raw, something true. "It’s funny," she continued, ignoring the way Blaine was watching her, his face unreadable, "how love is supposed to make you forget these things. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm stood there like America itself—a delusion wrapped in prettier lies, each one more fantastic than the last. The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm, a delusion. Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where wouldn't follow? History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not. And America, the grandest delusion of all, built on murder, theft, and the cruel arithmetic of slavery, is no exception. The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. written_by_MFA007.Original: Valentine farm is a delusion. Who told you the negro deserved a place of refuge? Who told you that you had that right? Every minute of your life’s suffering has argued otherwise. By every fact of history, it can’t exist. This place must be a delusion, too. Yet here we are.And America, too, is a delusion, the grandest one of all. The white race believes—believes with all its heart—that it is their right to take the land. To kill Indians. Make war. Enslave their brothers. This nation shouldn’t exist, if there is any justice in the world, for its foundations are murder, theft, and cruelty. Yet here we are.“I’m supposed to answer Mingo’s call for gradual progress, for closing our doors to those in need. I’m supposed to answer those who think this place is too close to the grievous influence of slavery, and that we should move west. I don’t have an answer for you. I don’t know what we should do. The word we. In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. It’s quite large. Brother Valentine has the maps of the world in his splendid library, you can look for yourself. They had different ways of subsistence, different customs, spoke a hundred different languages. And that great mixture was brought to America in the holds of slave ships. To the north, the south. Their sons and daughters picked tobacco, cultivated cotton, worked on the largest estates and smallest farms. We are craftsmen and midwives and preachers and peddlers. Black hands built the White House, the seat of our nation’s government. The word we. We are not one people but many different people. How can one person speak for this great, beautiful race—which is not one race but many, with a million desires and hopes and wishes for ourselves and our children?

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The old fisherman and his wife lived in Yeongdo, a small village near Busan. The couple was hardworking and pragmatic, and always sought new ways to bring money into their household. When the income from fish alone was no longer enough to sustain them, they decided to open their home to lodgers. The travelers passed through the village on the way to or back from Busan, and were always in need of a hot meal and a place to sleep. Both the travelers and the fisherman and his wife were happy for the company. As the years went by, the fisherman and his wife had three sons together. Only Hoonie, the eldest, survived. He was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot. Despite these challenges, Hoonie had a strong, stocky build and a kind, thoughtful nature. His shy voice and reserved manner of speech often caused people to underestimate his intelligence. In the face of teasing and mockery from people in the village, Hoonie remained diligent and mild-mannered. Elsewhere in the country, great turbulence was taking place. In 1910, Japan annexed Korea, and a tremendous political shift occurred. The fisherman and his wife were untroubled by the news. They didn't think it did any good to worry about how their aristocratic rulers had failed them. The decision-makers up in their high, gleaming chairs were as far removed from them as the moon. Meanwhile, there was still work to be done and bills to be paid. To keep up with the rising rent, the fisherman and his wife moved out of their bedroom in order to accommodate more lodgers. They even relocated their kitchen to the vegetable garden to make as much space as possible. Their home was a modest wooden structure with sliding paper doors and a clay-tiled roof. It had been built with the fisherman's own hands shortly before his marriage to his wife. In the heart of Busan, the luxurious mansion of the fisherman's landlord stood proud and stately. It had been assembled by hundreds of hands, and would one day be taken apart by hundreds more.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In 1910, when Japan annexed Korea, the aging fisherman and his wife rarely spoke of politics, focusing instead on the endless work of running their boardinghouse in Yeongdo, the small fishing village near Busan where they had lived all their lives. Their eldest son Hoonie, born with a cleft palate and twisted foot, had survived while his two younger brothers had not. The locals who didn't know him well often mistook his reserved manner of speaking for simplicity, but Hoonie's intelligence shone in his eyes, matched by his diligence and gentle nature. His parents had learned long ago not to waste energy lamenting what could not be changed – whether it was their son's conditions or the failures of their aristocratic rulers. When the rent increased again, they simply moved their own bedroom into the garden to make space for more lodgers, converting their former sleeping quarters into another room to let. Their kitchen now occupied a corner of the vegetable garden, the warm cooking smoke rising past clay roof tiles toward the evening sky. Some mornings, while preparing the lodgers' breakfast, the fisherman's wife would pause to watch the boats heading out to sea, their white sails bright against the gray dawn. She never envied the landlord's mansion in Busan with its Western furnishings and grand gates. Their modest wooden house with its sliding paper doors held everything they needed – space enough for lodgers whose rent helped them survive, a garden that provided vegetables for their soup, and most importantly, their son Hoonie, whose quiet strength and kind heart made their lives worth living. The other villagers often remarked on the family's fortitude, though the fisherman and his wife saw nothing remarkable in their way of life. To them, each day was simply another opportunity to work, to care for their son, and to maintain their dignity in a world that increasingly seemed to value only wealth and status. In Korea, as in most places, survival meant adapting to change without losing oneself, and this family had mastered that delicate balance through years of practiced resilience.

written_by_MFA029.Original: History has failed us, but no matter.At the turn of the century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. Both were born and raised in the fishing village of Yeongdo—a five-mile-wide islet beside the port city of Busan. In their long marriage, the wife gave birth to three sons, but only Hoonie, the eldest and the weakest one, survived. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot; he was, however, endowed with hefty shoulders, a squat build, and a golden complexion. Even as a young man, he retained the mild, thoughtful temperament he’d had as a child. When Hoonie covered his misshapen mouth with his hands, something he did out of habit meeting strangers, he resembled his nice-looking father, both having the same large, smiling eyes. Inky eyebrows graced his broad forehead, perpetually tanned from outdoor work. Like his parents, Hoonie was not a nimble talker, and some made the mistake of thinking that because he could not speak quickly there was something wrong with his mind, but that was not true.In 1910, when Hoonie was twenty-seven years old, Japan annexed Korea.The fisherman and his wife, thrifty and hardy peasants, refused to be distracted by the country’s incompetent aristocrats and corrupt rulers, who had lost their nation to thieves. When the rent for their house was raised again, the couple moved out of their bedroom and slept in the anteroom near the kitchen to increase the number of lodgers.The wooden house they had rented for over three decades was not large, just shy of five hundred square feet. Sliding paper doors divided the interior into three snug rooms, and the fisherman himself had replaced its leaky grass roof with reddish clay tiles to the benefit of his landlord, who lived in splendor in a mansion in Busan. Eventually, the kitchen was pushed out to the vegetable garden to make way for the larger cooking pots and the growing number of portable dining tables that hung on pegs along the mortared stone wall.

Instead, they remained focused on their immediate concerns, kept their heads low, and provided for one another as best they could. Hoonie stood and bowed toward the lodger, who returned a subtle look of pity, then avoided eye contact altogether. He was always hurt by these small gestures but was far too kind to allow those who hurt him to feel ashamed. It was easier that way.

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Hoonie was born in the final days of autumn, when the yellow gingko leaves scattered across the narrow village paths like golden scales. His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: Even before Japan annexed Korea, you could find the greatest expressions of both grief and resilience in small communities like Yeongdo, a small fishing village near Busan. There, a young fisherman found an equally hardworking, pragmatic wife, learned the different catches of the Yellow Sea’s shadowed and sunny areas, lost his country, had three sons, mourned two of them, and grew old. As displacement from military occupation spiked local rents, he and his wife set aside two rooms for lodgers. Despite the objective squalor of their situation and home—a modest wooden structure with a clay-tiled roof—the sliding paper doors of their boarding house became associated with safe harbor, gracious prices in slow fishing seasons, and cooking that made a wife seem unnecessary. When Korea was finally annexed in 1910, they gave up their bedroom, and even their kitchen, for more lodgers. The fishermen boarders relished the sight of the wife, seemingly unphased by the ruling class’s failures and unfolding political catastrophes, in the vegetable garden pickling vegetables and boiling soups with their catches. Over those meals, they got drunk, shouted banned songs from their youth, and mourned their country that the aristocrats had handed to a foreign emperor like a dowry without a groom. Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.

Even their landlord, who had kept his luxurious Busan mansion by donating an entire village’s homes to military occupation, came by one day to sample her maeuntang. Hoonie, the couple’s eldest and only surviving son was born with a cleft palate and twisted foot. However, the dire political and bodily circumstances Hoonie was born into instilled a quiet strength and clever adaptability. Some visitors from the mainland mistook his physical appearance and reserved speech for stupidity; his neighbors, though, often said, “Ki Hoonie will figure out with three limbs what you couldn’t with five.” Neighbors admired him as the kindest and most reliable man on the island, even as they decried the lack of marriageable men for their daughters. While his increasingly frail parents grew more desperate for a daughter-in-law, they secretly relished the diligent, undivided care Hoonie gave them and the boarding house.

His mother, exhausted but relieved, counted the boy's fingers and toes twice, then checked his face—there it was, the cleft that ran from his upper lip to his nose, a small but undeniable mark, alongside the twisted shape of his left foot. The midwife, wiping her hands on her apron, glanced at the father, who had not yet spoken. The fisherman nodded once and took his son in his arms. "Strong hands," he murmured, feeling the infant's tight grip around his finger. The family's house was a small wooden structure with sliding paper doors, perched near the docks where salt clung to the air. The rent had risen again, the landlord citing the increasing cost of maintaining the estate in Busan. In the mornings, she cooked rice gruel in the makeshift kitchen they had built in the vegetable garden, her breath visible in the early chill. "We should take in more lodgers," she said, ladling the porridge into bowls. Her husband chewed his millet slowly, nodding. Across the village, the Japanese officials had posted new notices, their blocky script announcing further changes, further restrictions. Some neighbors grumbled, others turned away, but the fisherman and his wife had no time for politics. When the younger sons were born, there had been celebrations, but only Hoonie lived to see his third birthday. By then, he had learned to walk, his gait uneven but determined, and to count to ten in both Korean and Japanese, as his father had insisted. "It will be useful," the fisherman had said, though he rarely spoke the occupiers' language himself. At night, the lodgers—traders from the markets, an out-of-work teacher, a widow with a sickly child—lay side by side on pallets spread across the common room, their breathing in sync with the waves outside. The house smelled of fish broth and damp wood, and from his corner, Hoonie listened to the murmurs of grown-ups, their words thick with worry, their voices low.

written_by_MFA031.Original: History has failed us, but no matter.At the turn of the century, an aging fisherman and his wife decided to take in lodgers for extra money. Both were born and raised in the fishing village of Yeongdo—a five-mile-wide islet beside the port city of Busan. In their long marriage, the wife gave birth to three sons, but only Hoonie, the eldest and the weakest one, survived. Hoonie was born with a cleft palate and a twisted foot; he was, however, endowed with hefty shoulders, a squat build, and a golden complexion. Even as a young man, he retained the mild, thoughtful temperament he’d had as a child. When Hoonie covered his misshapen mouth with his hands, something he did out of habit meeting strangers, he resembled his nice-looking father, both having the same large, smiling eyes. Inky eyebrows graced his broad forehead, perpetually tanned from outdoor work. Like his parents, Hoonie was not a nimble talker, and some made the mistake of thinking that because he could not speak quickly there was something wrong with his mind, but that was not true.In 1910, when Hoonie was twenty-seven years old, Japan annexed Korea.The fisherman and his wife, thrifty and hardy peasants, refused to be distracted by the country’s incompetent aristocrats and corrupt rulers, who had lost their nation to thieves. When the rent for their house was raised again, the couple moved out of their bedroom and slept in the anteroom near the kitchen to increase the number of lodgers.The wooden house they had rented for over three decades was not large, just shy of five hundred square feet. Sliding paper doors divided the interior into three snug rooms, and the fisherman himself had replaced its leaky grass roof with reddish clay tiles to the benefit of his landlord, who lived in splendor in a mansion in Busan. Eventually, the kitchen was pushed out to the vegetable garden to make way for the larger cooking pots and the growing number of portable dining tables that hung on pegs along the mortared stone wall.
